name: Fable-5 Web Development Prompt Library
description: 272 reusable prompt templates for web development, engineered per Claude Fable 5 capability analysis (Phase 1).

prompts.title: REST Resource Endpoint Set Design
prompts.description: Design a complete CRUD endpoint set for a single REST resource with correct HTTP semantics, an RFC 7807 error schema, and example payloads.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the REST endpoints for the {{resource}} resource in our {{service_name}} service.</goal>
<rationale>{{why these endpoints are needed and who consumes them}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT design endpoints outside the {{resource}} resource; note adjacent needs in a Notes section only.
- Do NOT invent fields; use only the attributes in the data model below.
- Follow HTTP semantics precisely: correct methods, correct status codes, no 200-for-everything.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Data model: {{attributes with types, required/optional, invariants}}
Existing conventions: {{paste of an existing endpoint doc to mirror, or 'none'}}
</context>

<contract>
Deliverable:
1. Endpoint table: method, path, purpose, request body/query params, success status + response body, error statuses.
2. Shared error schema for all endpoints using RFC 7807 problem details (type, title, status, detail, plus any extension members you justify).
3. Two example request/response pairs (one success, one error) as JSON.

Rules:
- Use 201 + Location header for creation, 200 for reads, 200/204 for updates/deletes (justify the choice), 404 for unknown ids, 409 for state conflicts, 422 only where validation cannot be expressed as 400.
- Do NOT add speculative fields ("might need later"); every field must trace to the data model or be flagged as an assumption in a separate list.
- Status codes must match RFC 9110 semantics; where a code's use is non-obvious, state the condition it signals.
- If the existing conventions doc conflicts with correct semantics, flag the conflict rather than silently copying the mistake.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every CRUD operation is reachable via exactly one endpoint; no duplicates, no gaps.
- Every endpoint lists at least one error case with its status and problem-details body.
- Zero invented resource attributes; assumptions listed separately from the contract.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Endpoint table (method/path/params/statuses), shared RFC 7807 error schema, and two JSON request/response examples with an assumptions list.

prompts.title: Pagination Strategy Decision (Cursor vs Offset)
prompts.description: Compare offset, cursor/keyset, and page-token pagination against real access patterns, then specify the full request/response contract for the winner.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Choose and specify a pagination strategy for the list endpoints of {{api_name}}.</goal>
<rationale>Clients must paginate {{entity}} collections reaching {{max_size}} rows; the wrong strategy causes skipped/duplicated rows or unacceptable latency at {{scale_condition}}.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT redesign endpoints beyond pagination parameters and the response envelope.
- Do NOT prescribe a strategy before comparing options.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Entities and access patterns: {{sort orders, filters, real-time vs static data}}
Client types: {{web dashboard / mobile infinite scroll / export jobs}}
Datastore: {{database + relevant indexes}}
Current behavior: {{existing pagination, or 'none'}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Decision table comparing offset/limit, cursor (keyset), and page-token approaches: pros, cons, and a concrete failure mode for each under our access patterns; weighted by {{criteria: write-consistency, deep-page latency, client simplicity, export use case}}.
2. One recommendation plus the single criterion that decided it; push back if my stated constraints point elsewhere.
3. Full request/response contract for the chosen strategy: query parameters (names, defaults, max page size), response envelope (data, cursor/has_more), and boundary behavior (empty page, invalid cursor, cursor pointing at a deleted row).
4. Error cases: status code and problem-details body for an invalid or expired cursor, with justification.

Rules:
- Performance claims must tie to the datastore behavior above (e.g. OFFSET scan cost), not generic assertions; mark anything unverified as ASSUMPTION.
- Do NOT invent response fields beyond the contract.

Acceptance criteria:
- Decision table covers all three strategies with at least one failure mode each.
- Contract specifies behavior for all three listed boundary conditions.
- Backward compatibility with {{current_behavior}} is stated explicitly: breaking or not, and why.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Weighted decision table across three pagination strategies, a defended recommendation, and the chosen strategy's full request/response and error contract.

prompts.title: Uniform RFC 7807 Error Model
prompts.description: Design one problem-details error schema plus an error catalog mapping every endpoint failure to a status, type URI, and redaction policy.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design a uniform error model for {{api_name}} and apply it to the endpoints listed below.</goal>
<rationale>Clients currently cannot distinguish {{failure modes, e.g. validation vs conflict vs upstream failure}} programmatically, forcing fragile message-string parsing.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT change success responses or endpoint paths.
- Do NOT invent new HTTP status codes or repurpose standard ones contrary to RFC 9110 semantics.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Endpoints in scope: {{list}}
Current error behavior: {{paste real responses verbatim — do not paraphrase}}
</context>

<contract>
1. A single problem-details schema (RFC 7807, updated by RFC 9457): media type application/problem+json, members type/title/status/detail/instance, plus extension members only where justified (e.g. an 'errors' array for field-level validation, 'trace_id').
2. Error catalog table: each failure condition -> status code -> type URI -> whether 'detail' may be shown to end users. Cover at minimum: validation, authentication, authorization, not-found, conflict, rate-limit, upstream dependency failure.
3. One example JSON body for the three most common errors.
4. Migration note: what changes for existing clients, if anything.

Rules:
- 4xx/5xx bodies must not leak stack traces, SQL, or internal hostnames; state exactly what gets redacted.
- 401 vs 403 vs 404: state which existence-disclosure policy you applied and why, then apply it consistently.
- If current behavior already conforms somewhere, say so instead of rewriting it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every endpoint in scope maps every documented failure to the catalog.
- Every status used is a standard code whose semantics match its definition.
- No schema field appears without a stated consumer need.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Problem-details JSON schema, failure-to-status error catalog with redaction policy, three example error bodies, and a client migration note.

prompts.title: Idempotent POST Endpoint Design
prompts.description: Add safe-retry semantics to a non-idempotent POST endpoint: Idempotency-Key validation, storage, conflict rules, concurrency handling, and anchored handler edits.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Add idempotent submission semantics to {{operation, e.g. POST /payments}} so clients can safely retry after timeouts.</goal>
<rationale>{{what goes wrong today: duplicate charges / double-created orders on client retries}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT change the success payload shape or other endpoints.
- Do NOT add dependencies; if one seems required, list it in Notes with justification instead.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Stack: {{framework, ORM, datastore with versions}}
Existing handler: {{paste or reference file}}
Storage available for idempotency records: {{table / cache / none yet}}
Client retry behavior: {{SDK retry policy, timeout values}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Design: Idempotency-Key header validation (format, required vs optional), what is stored (key, request hash, response snapshot, expiry), and conflict rules — same key + same payload replays the stored response; same key + different payload returns a status you choose (recommend between 409 and 422) with justification.
2. Concurrency handling: behavior when two requests with the same key arrive simultaneously; name the mechanism (row lock or unique constraint) appropriate to the datastore above.
3. Failure taxonomy: which failures are safe to retry with the same key (network timeout, 5xx, 429) and which are not (4xx validation), and what the client observes in each case.
4. Implementation as anchored edits to the existing handler (FILE / verbatim ANCHOR / replacement blocks), minimal diff.

Rules:
- Do NOT mark downstream calls as safe without evidence; list each downstream call with its idempotency guarantee or mark UNKNOWN.
- Key expiry/TTL must be justified against client retry windows, not picked arbitrarily.

Acceptance criteria:
- Replay of identical key+payload returns identical status and body.
- Same key + divergent payload is rejected with the specified status.
- Concurrent duplicate submissions produce exactly one side effect.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Idempotency design (key validation, storage, conflict rules, concurrency mechanism), retry failure taxonomy, and minimal anchored handler edits.

prompts.title: GraphQL Domain Schema Design
prompts.description: Design SDL types, queries, and mutations for one domain from a data model and named client operations, with explicit nullability and mutation-payload decisions.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the GraphQL schema (types, queries, mutations, inputs) for the {{domain}} domain of {{app_name}}.</goal>
<rationale>{{who queries it and which screens/operations it powers}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT model domains outside {{domain}}; record adjacent needs under Notes only.
- Do NOT invent entity attributes beyond the data model below.
- Follow the GraphQL specification's type system; leave no custom scalar's semantics undefined.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Data model: {{entities, fields, relationships, nullability invariants}}
Client operations needed: {{screens/use cases with the data each requires}}
Existing schema conventions: {{paste an SDL excerpt to mirror, or 'none'}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Complete SDL: object types, input types, queries, mutations; connection patterns (edges/node/pageInfo) for any list that can grow unbounded.
2. Nullability decision table: for each non-obvious nullable field, why it is nullable (genuine data absence vs error recovery), preferring non-null where the invariant holds.
3. Mutation design: each mutation returns a payload type containing the mutated object plus a typed user-errors field; explain this choice versus surfacing everything as top-level errors.
4. Example operation documents for the two most important client use cases.

Rules:
- Do NOT expose storage internals (join tables, foreign-key naming) as schema shape unless a client need justifies it.
- No field without a named consumer from the operation list; speculative fields go in Notes.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every listed client operation is expressible in a single query or mutation without under-fetching.
- SDL is valid GraphQL and follows {{naming convention}} consistently; state how you validated it or mark UNVALIDATED.
- Every custom scalar has a one-line serialization definition.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Complete valid SDL for the domain, a nullability decision table, typed-error mutation payloads, and two example operation documents.

prompts.title: N+1 Resolver Audit and Batching Fix
prompts.description: Diagnose evidence-backed N+1 query patterns in resolvers and fix them with minimal diffs (DataLoader/prefetch) without changing schema or response shape.
prompts.prompt: Find and fix N+1 query patterns in the resolvers below without changing the schema or returned data. {{observed symptom with evidence, e.g. p95 on Query.orders with 50 rows and its query-log excerpt}} - Do NOT change the GraphQL schema, resolver signatures, or response shape. - Do NOT refactor unrelated resolvers; list other issues in Notes without fixing them. {{server runtime, ORM + version, DataLoader version or 'none'}} {{implicated resolvers and data-access functions, verbatim}} {{query logs or tracing output showing repeated queries, verbatim}} 1. Diagnosis table: each N+1 site -> triggering field -> why the N+1 occurs (which resolution layer) -> fix mechanism (DataLoader batching, join/prefetch) with a one-line justification. 2. Fixes as anchored search/replace blocks (FILE / verbatim ANCHOR / replacement), minimal diff, following the batching pattern in {{reference_file}} if one is provided; do not introduce a batching style that appears nowhere in the codebase. 3. Verification plan: the exact operation and instrumentation proving the query count dropped, e.g. "operation X issues at most K SQL statements regardless of list size." Rules: - Distinguish request-scoped batching (DataLoader per-request cache) from cross-request caching; do not add a cross-request cache over mutable data without flagging staleness. - If code inspection suggests an N+1 the evidence does not show, label it SUSPECTED, not confirmed. - Fix the smallest set of resolvers that eliminates the evidenced N+1s. Acceptance criteria: - Every evidence-backed N+1 has a corresponding fix. - No schema or response-shape changes. - Verification plan is executable and states the expected query-count bound.
prompts.expectedOutput: N+1 diagnosis table tied to verbatim query-log evidence, minimal anchored fixes, and an executable verification plan with a query-count bound.

prompts.title: GraphQL Schema Change Safety Audit
prompts.description: Classify every diff between current and proposed SDL by breaking-change risk using client usage analytics, and produce a shippable corrected SDL.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Audit the proposed GraphQL schema changes for breaking behavior and classify each change's safety before release.</goal>
<rationale>Mobile clients at version {{min_supported_version}} cannot be force-upgraded; a breaking schema change silently crashes shipped apps.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT redesign the schema; classify changes and, where unsafe, propose the smallest safe alternative.
- Do NOT assume client usage beyond the analytics below; unknowns are UNKNOWN, not safe.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Current SDL: {{paste}}
Proposed SDL: {{paste}}
Client operation analytics: {{fields actually queried per client/version, or 'unavailable'}}
Deprecation policy: {{policy text}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Change classification table: each schema diff entry -> category (dangerous: field/type removal, type change, nullability tightening, argument removal; safe: purely additive; safe-with-deprecation) -> evidence (which client operations reference it, or UNKNOWN) -> action (ship / deprecate-first / reject).
2. For every deprecate-first item: the @deprecated directive with reason text, the replacement, and the minimum deprecation window from the policy.
3. For every UNKNOWN item: the exact data needed to resolve it and the interim safe decision.
4. Corrected proposed SDL containing only changes classified ship or deprecate-first.

Rules:
- Apply the GraphQL spec's notion of breaking changes; do not invent categories.
- Tightening nullability on output positions and loosening it on input positions must each be classified explicitly — they are not symmetric.
- Evidence over assumption: a change is "safe" only if analytics show zero references or the change is purely additive.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every diff entry appears in the classification table with evidence.
- No removal ships without a deprecation window unless zero referenced usage is evidenced.
- The corrected SDL keeps every currently queried field available, or deprecates it.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Evidence-backed change classification table, @deprecated annotations with windows, UNKNOWN resolution list, and a corrected shippable SDL.

prompts.title: API Versioning Strategy Selection
prompts.description: Compare URL-path, header/media-type, and additive-only evolution strategies against consumer constraints, then write the versioning policy.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Choose an API versioning strategy for {{api_name}} and write the versioning policy.</goal>
<rationale>{{context: first public API / existing unversioned API with N consumers / internal-only}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT design endpoint details; this decision covers version mechanics and policy only.
- Do NOT recommend before enumerating options.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Consumers: {{count, internal/external, update cadence, can we contact them directly?}}
Expected change frequency: {{how often breaking changes are anticipated}}
Platform constraints: {{gateway/CDN capabilities, SDK generation}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Decision table of three options — URL path versioning, header/media-type versioning, and no-explicit-versioning with additive-only evolution: pros, cons, and how each fails under our consumer constraints; weighted by {{criteria}}.
2. One recommendation plus the criterion that decided it; if my stated constraints contradict your pick, say so explicitly.
3. Versioning policy document: operational definitions of breaking vs non-breaking change (explicit checkable lists), version support lifetime, announcement channel, and what old-version requests receive after end-of-life (exact status code + body).
4. One worked example of a breaking change handled end-to-end under the recommended strategy.

Rules:
- "Breaking" must be defined operationally — client code that worked stops working — not vaguely.
- Do NOT claim any strategy is "RESTful-correct"; evaluate on operational evidence only.
- If clients already call the API, their migration path is mandatory content, not optional.

Acceptance criteria:
- All three options compared with at least one failure mode each.
- Policy includes checkable definitions of breaking and non-breaking.
- End-of-life behavior specifies the exact status code and body shape.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Weighted decision table of three versioning strategies, a defended recommendation, and a versioning policy with checkable breaking-change definitions.

prompts.title: Endpoint Deprecation and Sunset Plan
prompts.description: Produce an evidence-based deprecation timeline with RFC 9745 Deprecation and RFC 8594 Sunset signaling, migration guide skeleton, and enforcement plan.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a deprecation and sunset plan for {{endpoint_or_field}}.</goal>
<rationale>{{why it is being retired and what replaces it}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT deprecate anything else; related candidates go in Notes only.
- Do NOT set dates unsupported by the usage data below; if data is missing, mark the date BLOCKED with the data needed.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Usage analytics: {{request volume by consumer/version over the last N days}}
Replacement: {{new endpoint/field and its behavior differences}}
Support commitments: {{SLAs, contracts, public documentation promises}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Timeline table: announcement date, deprecation-signal start, sunset date, hard removal — each justified against the usage analytics and support commitments.
2. Signaling plan: response headers (Deprecation per RFC 9745 carrying the deprecation timestamp; Sunset per RFC 8594 carrying the HTTP-date of removal; Link header to migration docs), documentation changes, and direct consumer notification — with exact example header values.
3. Migration guide skeleton: before/after request examples showing every behavior difference, including cases where the replacement is not a drop-in.
4. Enforcement plan: what requests receive after sunset (e.g. 410 Gone with a problem-details body pointing at migration docs, or an alternative — justify), plus monitoring to detect remaining callers before removal.

Rules:
- Sunset must not precede the end of any evidenced support window; flag conflicts instead of scheduling over them.
- Deprecation signaling must keep old behavior fully functioning; do not degrade it early as "nudging."
- Every date traces to evidence or is marked BLOCKED.

Acceptance criteria:
- Deprecation and Sunset headers appear with syntactically valid example values.
- Migration guide covers every documented behavior difference.
- The plan names the metric proving removal is safe (e.g. zero requests from supported consumers for N consecutive days).
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Evidence-justified deprecation timeline, exact Deprecation/Sunset header signaling, migration guide skeleton, and post-sunset enforcement plan.

prompts.title: OpenAPI Diff Breaking-Change Impact Audit
prompts.description: Classify every change between two OpenAPI specs by compatibility with quoted evidence, quantify consumer impact, and propose compatible remediations.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Audit the diff between the current and proposed OpenAPI specs, classify every change by compatibility, and quantify consumer impact.</goal>
<rationale>{{why the change set is being made; which consumers are pinned to the current contract}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT restructure the API beyond classifying the given diff and flagging unsafe entries.
- Do NOT classify by intuition; every verdict must cite the spec elements involved.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Current spec: {{OpenAPI 3.1 document}}
Proposed spec: {{OpenAPI 3.1 document}}
Consumer inventory: {{generated SDKs, known integrators, mobile app versions}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Coverage matrix: every changed path/operation/schema/property -> change type (removed, type-narrowed, required-added, enum-shrunk, response-changed, security-changed, other) -> verdict (breaking / non-breaking / context-dependent) -> quoted spec fragments as evidence.
2. For context-dependent items: the exact condition that decides the verdict (e.g. "breaking only for clients that strictly validate unknown enum values").
3. Impact summary: which consumers from the inventory are affected per breaking item, or UNKNOWN with the data required.
4. Remediation list: the smallest change to the proposed spec converting each breaking item into compatible evolution (e.g. add new field + deprecate old instead of rename).

Rules:
- Adding a required request property is breaking; making a response property nullable breaks strictly typed clients — classify both explicitly, never as "minor."
- Renaming is removal plus addition; treat it as such.
- If the diff tool output and your reading conflict, quote both and flag rather than silently choosing.

Acceptance criteria:
- 100% of diff entries appear in the matrix; none skipped as "trivial."
- Every breaking verdict names the consumer-facing failure it causes.
- Every breaking item has a remediation or an explicit justification for breaking intentionally.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Complete change coverage matrix with quoted evidence and verdicts, per-consumer impact summary, and compatible-evolution remediations.

prompts.title: Rate-Limit Policy and HTTP Contract Design
prompts.description: Derive numeric rate limits from traffic evidence and specify the full 429 contract: Retry-After, problem-details body, disclosure headers, and client retry guidance.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the rate-limiting policy and its HTTP contract for {{api_name}}.</goal>
<rationale>{{what abuse or load it must prevent; which legitimate burst patterns must keep working}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT design enforcement infrastructure internals; contract and policy only (algorithm choice is in scope, stack selection is not).
- Do NOT pick numeric limits without deriving them from the usage data below.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Legitimate traffic profile: {{requests/sec per consumer type, burst shapes}}
Abuse/failure scenarios: {{scraping, credential stuffing, retry storms}}
Capacity ceiling: {{backend sustainable RPS, per-dependency limits}}
Client types: {{browser, server-to-server, mobile}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Limit table: per consumer class -> limit, window, burst allowance, scope (per API key / per user / per IP) — each number derived from the data above, derivation shown.
2. HTTP contract: 429 rejection with Retry-After (delta-seconds and/or HTTP-date), application/problem+json body; evaluate the IETF RateLimit header fields draft against conventional X-RateLimit-* headers and pick one with justification.
3. Behavior specification: what counts toward the limit (failed auth? other 4xx? streaming responses?) and enforcement ordering vs authentication, with reasons.
4. Client retry guidance: exact jittered exponential backoff recipe that honors Retry-After and resists retry storms.
5. Legitimate-burst analysis: for each known burst pattern, show numerically that it passes or gets a documented exception.

Rules:
- 429 must not fire on the evidenced legitimate traffic profile; prove it with numbers.
- Error bodies and headers expose policy only, never internal capacity figures.
- Insufficient data -> output BLOCKED with the exact measurement needed; never invent a number.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every limit traces to a derivation or is marked provisional with a measurement plan.
- Contract includes one complete 429 example response (headers + body).
- Retry guidance is specific enough to implement without further decisions.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Derived per-class limit table, complete 429 + Retry-After + problem-details contract, header-format decision, and storm-safe client retry recipe.

prompts.title: Rate-Limiter Algorithm and Multi-Tenant Fairness
prompts.description: Compare five rate-limiting algorithms with quantified edge behavior, then design noisy-neighbor fairness, distributed enforcement, and degradation policy.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Select rate-limiting algorithms and a fairness design for {{system}}, a multi-tenant API under {{load profile}}.</goal>
<rationale>{{incident or risk: noisy-neighbor starvation, post-outage thundering herd, cost amplification}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT select infrastructure vendors; algorithm and policy level only.
- Do NOT assert performance characteristics qualitatively; tie each claim to a mechanism (memory per key, window-edge behavior, clock-skew sensitivity).
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Tenancy model: {{tenant counts, tiers, per-tier entitlements}}
Traffic characteristics: {{arrival distribution, burst causes, attack history}}
Deployment shape: {{single/multi-region, where limits can be enforced}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Decision table comparing fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter, token bucket, and leaky bucket: pros, cons, memory cost per tracked key, burst behavior at window edges, and failure mode under our traffic; weighted by {{criteria}}.
2. Recommendation (single algorithm or layered) with the deciding criterion.
3. Fairness design: how one tenant's flood is prevented from consuming shared capacity (per-tenant quotas, concurrency limits, queue isolation) and what well-behaved tenants are guaranteed during an attack, stated as guarantees with mechanisms.
4. Distributed-enforcement analysis: local-approximate vs centralized-exact counting, their over/under-admission error, and which is acceptable per tier.
5. Degradation plan: fail-open vs fail-closed when the rate-limit store is down, per endpoint class, with the risk each accepts.

Rules:
- Quantify approximation claims (e.g. fixed window admits up to 2x at window boundaries).
- No fairness guarantee without a mechanism beside it; label unproven guarantees OPEN QUESTIONS.
- Every recommendation names its own worst-case failure.

Acceptance criteria:
- All five algorithms compared with quantified edge behavior.
- Fairness section contains at least one hard guarantee plus its mechanism.
- Degradation plan picks fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint class with justification.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Quantified five-algorithm decision table, layered recommendation, mechanism-backed fairness guarantees, distributed-counting analysis, and fail-open/closed plan.

prompts.title: OpenAPI 3.1 Document Authoring
prompts.description: Author a valid OpenAPI 3.1 document from an endpoint list with reusable components, shared problem-details errors, and a TODO list instead of invented content.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Author an OpenAPI 3.1 document for the endpoints described below.</goal>
<rationale>{{purpose: SDK codegen / docs portal / contract review}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT document endpoints not listed below.
- Do NOT invent fields, status codes, or examples not derivable from the endpoint descriptions; undetermined items go in a TODO list, never silently into the spec.
- Target OpenAPI 3.1 exactly (JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect); do not use 3.0-only constructs such as nullable: true — use type arrays instead.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Endpoints: {{method, path, purpose, request fields, response fields, auth requirement — one per line}}
Auth scheme: {{bearer JWT / API key / OAuth2 flows}}
Base URLs: {{servers}}
</context>

<contract>
1. One valid OpenAPI 3.1 YAML document: info, servers, security schemes, paths with operations, reusable components/schemas, and shared error responses via $ref.
2. Every operation has: operationId ({{naming convention}}), summary, parameters, requestBody where applicable, success response plus the error set, and one request example + one response example.
3. Error responses use application/problem+json with a shared ProblemDetail schema.
4. A short TODO list of anything the endpoint descriptions left undetermined.

Rules:
- Field names, types, and required lists must match the endpoint descriptions exactly; flag contradictions instead of silently resolving them.
- No placeholder descriptions like "string"; write real descriptions or move the item to TODO.
- Reuse schemas through components; never inline-duplicate.

Acceptance criteria:
- The document parses as valid OpenAPI 3.1 — state how you validated it, or mark UNVALIDATED.
- Every listed endpoint appears exactly once; zero extras.
- Every operation defines at least one non-2xx response.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Valid OpenAPI 3.1 YAML with reusable components, problem-details error responses, per-operation examples, and an explicit TODO list of undetermined details.

prompts.title: OpenAPI Spec Audit and Mechanical Fix
prompts.description: Audit an OpenAPI document with an evidence-backed findings table and executed checklist, fixing only mechanical errors via anchored edits.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Audit this OpenAPI document for correctness, completeness, and internal consistency; report findings, then fix only the mechanical errors.</goal>
<rationale>{{what the spec feeds: generated SDKs / docs / gateway validation — and what breaks when it is wrong}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT redesign the API or rename operations/paths in the fix pass; design concerns are reported, not fixed.
- Do NOT add endpoints or fields not already implied by the document.
</boundaries>
</task>

<spec>{{paste the OpenAPI document verbatim}}</spec>
<context>{{how the spec is produced (hand-written / generated from {{framework}}) and what validates it today, if anything}}</context>

<contract>
1. Findings table: location -> category (spec violation / inconsistency / missing error coverage / doc quality) -> evidence (quote the offending fragment) -> severity (breaks tooling / breaks clients / cosmetic) -> fix or recommendation.
2. Executed checklist, each row PASS/FAIL with evidence: valid against the declared OpenAPI version; every $ref resolves; operationIds unique; every operation has at least one error response; required lists consistent with defined properties; examples valid against their schemas; security requirements reference defined schemes.
3. Corrected spec containing ONLY mechanical fixes (broken $refs, type errors, invalid examples) as anchored search/replace blocks.
4. Open questions list for findings needing the API owner's decision.

Rules:
- Evidence over assertion: no finding without a quoted location.
- If you cannot validate with a real tool, state UNVALIDATED and say which checks were manual.
- Do NOT report style preferences as defects.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every checklist row has explicit PASS/FAIL with evidence.
- Fixes are limited to the mechanical category; everything else is a recommendation.
- No content invented to fill gaps — gaps become open questions.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Quoted-evidence findings table, executed PASS/FAIL checklist, mechanical-only anchored fixes, and an open-questions list.

prompts.title: Spec-vs-Implementation Drift Detection
prompts.description: Verify a live API against its OpenAPI contract with executed requests and produce an evidence-backed CONFORMS/DRIFT/UNVERIFIED matrix.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Verify that the live implementation of {{api_name}} conforms to its OpenAPI contract, and produce an evidence-backed drift report.</goal>
<rationale>{{what depends on the contract: client SDKs, partner integrations; the cost of drift}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT fix the implementation or the spec; report and classify drift only, with a recommended owner per item.
- Do NOT claim conformance for anything not actually exercised; untested means UNVERIFIED.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Spec: {{path or pasted OpenAPI document}}
Implementation: {{repo path / route files / running base URL}}
Available tooling: {{test runner, HTTP client, schema-validation library}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Test plan: for each operation, the requests needed to exercise the success case and every documented error case, with response schema validation against the spec.
2. Drift matrix: operation -> check (path exists / method / request validation / response schema / error shape / auth) -> CONFORMS / DRIFT / UNVERIFIED -> verbatim evidence (request + response, or command + output).
3. Drift classification per item: implementation-wrong, spec-wrong, or ambiguous — with reasoning.
4. Recommended fix owner and minimal correction per drift item (no code changes in this pass).

Rules:
- Every CONFORMS verdict requires executed-request evidence; code reading alone yields UNVERIFIED.
- Probe the edge cases the spec implies: missing required fields, wrong types, unknown enum values, unauthorized access — record actual behavior even where the spec is silent.
- Where the spec is silent but the implementation behaves consistently, mark spec-gap, not drift.

Acceptance criteria:
- 100% of operations appear in the matrix; none omitted.
- No CONFORMS verdict without attached verbatim evidence.
- Every DRIFT has a classification and a proposed owner.
- The report ends with DONE / NOT DONE against this contract.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Per-operation test plan, evidence-backed CONFORMS/DRIFT/UNVERIFIED matrix, drift classifications with owners, and a DONE/NOT DONE verdict.

prompts.title: Outbound Webhook Delivery Contract
prompts.description: Design the full webhook contract: event envelope, HMAC signature scheme, retry policy with honest delivery guarantees, and a receiver verification snippet.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the outbound webhook contract for {{events, e.g. payment.succeeded}} in {{product}}.</goal>
<rationale>{{who receives these webhooks and what they build on them}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT design event-producing internals beyond what the contract requires.
- Do NOT invent event types; cover only the events listed below.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Events and available payloads: {{event types + the data each can carry}}
Receiver profile: {{technical sophistication, languages, firewall constraints}}
Delivery requirements: {{ordering needs, latency SLO, volume}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Event envelope schema (JSON): id, type, created (state the timestamp format), data, and an API-version field — with nullability and one worked example per event type.
2. Delivery contract: HTTP method, headers, timeout, expected receiver behavior (2xx = acknowledged; anything else = retry), and the acknowledgment deadline.
3. Security: HMAC-SHA256 signature scheme — exact signed-string construction, header name, timestamp inclusion with a replay window, and key rotation procedure; IP allowlisting only as an optional second layer.
4. Retry policy: schedule (initial delay, backoff factor, max attempts, jitter), terminal-failure handling, and how receivers replay missed events.
5. Receiver-side contract: idempotent processing keyed on event id; state explicitly whether ordering is guaranteed (with why) and document duplicate delivery as possible.
6. Receiver verification snippet in {{language}} showing signature validation and the idempotency check.

Rules:
- No delivery guarantee the retry policy does not actually provide.
- Secret material never appears in payloads or logs; state the redaction rule.
- Versioning rule in the contract: additive payload changes only within a version; breaking changes require a new version.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every listed event has a complete example payload.
- Signature construction is specified precisely enough to implement independently in two languages.
- Duplicate and out-of-order delivery are both addressed with receiver instructions.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Event envelope schema with examples, precise HMAC signature scheme, retry/jitter policy with honest guarantees, and a receiver verification snippet.

prompts.title: Event Schema Evolution and Compatibility Governance
prompts.description: Choose a compatibility mode and governance workflow so producers can evolve event schemas without breaking pinned consumers, with checkable change-classification rules.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the evolution strategy for {{event_stream_name}} event schemas so producers can change payloads without breaking deployed consumers.</goal>
<rationale>{{current pain: coupled deploys, consumer breakage incidents, schema sprawl}}</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT select or evaluate message-broker vendors; schema-governance level only (registry adoption is in scope as a tradeoff).
- Do NOT assume consumers can be redeployed; treat them as pinned.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Events in scope: {{types and current schemas}}
Consumer landscape: {{count, languages, teams, unknown external consumers?}}
Serialization: {{JSON / Avro / Protobuf}}; transport: {{for context only, not redesign}}
Registry: {{existing schema registry or 'none'}}
</context>

<contract>
1. Compatibility decision table: backward / forward / full / none — what each permits, what breaks without it, failure modes in our consumer landscape; weighted by {{criteria: consumer diversity, change frequency, tooling maturity}}. One recommendation with the deciding criterion.
2. Change classification rules for the chosen serialization: whether each operation (add optional field, remove field, rename, type-widen, add enum value, change default) is safe under the chosen mode — a checkable list for code review.
3. Governance workflow: how a proposed schema change gets validated (registry check / CI contract test), approved, and rolled out — including the unknown-field tolerance rule and the danger of extending closed sets like enums.
4. Versioning scheme: schema version vs event-type version vs payload-level version field — pick one and justify.
5. Consumer-driven contract testing: the minimum contract tests consumers publish and producers run before merge.

Rules:
- Every "safe" classification must be qualified by the serialization's actual semantics (e.g. strictly validating JSON consumers are not covered by backward-compatible claims).
- Unknown-consumer risk must be addressed explicitly; "we think nobody uses it" is not evidence.
- No guarantee without a named enforcement mechanism (CI gate, registry rule) beside it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Decision table covers all four compatibility modes.
- Change classification list is mechanically checkable in review.
- Governance workflow names the artifact that blocks an incompatible change.
- Rollback: how a bad schema deploy is contained, stated concretely.
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Four-mode compatibility decision table, checkable change-classification rules, CI/registry governance workflow, versioning scheme, and contract-test minimums.

prompts.title: Greenfield System Decomposition from a Product Brief
prompts.description: Turn a raw product brief into a first-pass system decomposition: candidate component maps, responsibilities, and a recommended starting architecture sized to the actual team and scale.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a first-pass system decomposition for {{product_brief}} so that a team of {{team_size}} can start building within one sprint.</goal>
<rationale>Early decomposition mistakes are the most expensive to reverse; I need explicit options and a justified recommendation, not a default diagram.</rationale>
<context>
- Expected scale: {{target_users_scale}} (e.g. "5k MAU, ~20 req/s peak")
- Hard constraints: {{hard_constraints}} (budget, compliance, existing stack, deadlines)
</context>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT default to microservices, Kubernetes, or a service mesh; justify any distributed component against the stated scale.
- Do NOT claim the design "scales infinitely" or "handles any load" — every scalability statement must cite a number from the context or be flagged as an unverified assumption.
- Do NOT select specific vendor products; stay at component-type level (e.g. "relational DB", "object storage").
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A decomposition proposal containing:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Two candidate decompositions (e.g. modular monolith vs. split services), each with: a mermaid component diagram, a responsibility table (| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Talks to |), pros, cons, and how it fails.
2. A decision matrix weighted by: team size, time-to-first-release, operational burden, expected scale.
3. One recommendation, the criterion that decided it, and what evidence would change your mind.
4. An "Assumptions" list — every capacity or traffic number you assumed because I did not provide it.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Exactly 2 decompositions compared, each with pros/cons and a failure mode.
- Mermaid diagram parses (balanced subgraph brackets, no undefined nodes).
- Every numeric claim traces to my context or appears in the Assumptions list.
- Recommendation names a single deciding criterion.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Two decomposition options each with mermaid diagram, responsibility table, pros/cons/failure mode, a weighted decision matrix, one recommendation with deciding criterion, and an explicit assumptions list.

prompts.title: Decompose an Existing Module into Components with Clean Interfaces
prompts.description: Restructure a tangled module or feature into named components with explicit interfaces and dependency direction, comparing at least two decomposition axes before recommending one.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Propose a decomposition of {{existing_module_description}} into cohesive components with explicit interfaces, so that {{primary_pain_point}} is eliminated.</goal>
<rationale>The module has become a change-amplification point; every modification touches unrelated code and review cycles are slowing.</rationale>
<context>
- Current structure: {{code_excerpt_or_tree}}
- Pain points observed: {{pain_points}}
- Invariants that must be preserved: {{invariants}} (public APIs, behaviors, performance budgets)
</context>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT propose a rewrite; decomposition must be reachable via incremental, individually shippable moves.
- Do NOT introduce new external dependencies or frameworks.
- Do NOT redesign parts of the system outside the named module; if you spot adjacent problems, list them under "Notes" without designing fixes.
- Respect the stated invariants as binding.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A decomposition plan with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Two decomposition options cut along different axes (e.g. by domain capability vs. by technical layer), each with: component list, one-line responsibility per component, interface signatures (types, not implementations), dependency direction, pros, cons, and failure mode.
2. A decision matrix weighted by {{decision_criteria}} (e.g. blast radius of future changes, testability, migration effort).
3. Recommendation + the criterion that decided it.
4. An ordered migration sequence of small moves, each preserving the invariants.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Both options keep every stated invariant intact.
- No circular dependencies between proposed components (state the direction explicitly).
- Each migration step is independently shippable.
- Notes section lists adjacent issues without fixing them.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Two decomposition options along different axes with components, typed interfaces, dependency direction, pros/cons/failure modes, a weighted decision matrix, a recommendation, and an incremental migration sequence.

prompts.title: Capacity-Informed System Design with Explicit Assumption Flags
prompts.description: Full system design for a stated workload where every capacity number is either derived from provided data or explicitly flagged as an assumption, with two or three competing topologies compared.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the system architecture for {{system_brief}} that meets a latency budget of {{latency_budget}} under {{traffic_assumptions}} with data growing at {{data_growth}}.</goal>
<rationale>This design will be reviewed by staff engineers and used for a build/no-build decision; unquantified claims or hidden assumptions will discredit it.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Show back-of-envelope capacity math (requests/sec, storage/year, bandwidth) for every sizing decision.
- Every number not derivable from my inputs must appear in an Assumptions table with a sensitivity note ("if this is 10x off, X changes").
- Do NOT claim linear scalability, "infinite" scale, or zero-downtime anything without stating the mechanism and its limit.
- Do NOT pad the design with components whose absence would not violate a stated requirement — no resume-driven architecture.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A design document containing:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Capacity model: derived load numbers with the arithmetic shown.
2. Two or three candidate topologies, each with a mermaid diagram, data-flow description, pros, cons, and the failure mode that hurts most.
3. A tradeoff matrix weighted by {{decision_criteria}} (e.g. latency headroom, operational cost, team cognitive load, growth headroom).
4. Recommendation with the deciding criterion, plus the cheapest load test that would validate or kill it.
5. Assumptions table: | Assumption | Value used | Sensitivity if wrong |.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every sizing number traces to my inputs or the assumptions table.
- Each option names at least one concrete failure mode.
- The recommended design includes a validation load test with a pass/fail threshold.
- No component lacks a requirement justifying it.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A capacity model with shown arithmetic, 2-3 topologies with mermaid diagrams and pros/cons/failure modes, a weighted tradeoff matrix, a recommendation with a validation load test, and a sensitivity-flagged assumptions table.

prompts.title: Service Boundary Identification via Domain Decomposition
prompts.description: Find candidate service boundaries in a domain by comparing capability-based and data-ownership-based cuts, with coupling analysis to expose which boundary set will hurt least.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Identify candidate service boundaries for {{domain_description}} that minimize cross-service coupling for the changes we actually make.</goal>
<rationale>Wrong boundaries create distributed-monolith pain: every feature becomes a multi-service coordinated release. I need the coupling exposed before any code moves.</rationale>
<context>
- Core entities: {{entity_list}}
- Business capabilities: {{business_capabilities}}
- What changes often vs. rarely: {{change_frequency_notes}}
- Team topology: {{team_topology}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Boundaries must follow change patterns and data ownership, not entity-per-service orthodoxy.
- Do NOT propose any infrastructure (brokers, gateways, meshes) — this is a boundary analysis, not a deployment design.
- Do NOT exceed {{max_services}} candidate services; fewer is a feature.
- Flag any boundary whose justification rests on "it might need to scale independently" without evidence.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A boundary analysis with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Two candidate boundary maps (e.g. cut by business capability vs. cut by data ownership/lifecycle), each as: service list with owned data and exposed operations, plus a mermaid interaction diagram.
2. Coupling table per option: | Service pair | Shared data? | Sync calls needed? | Change-frequency overlap |.
3. Pros, cons, and the failure mode of each map (what painful scenario does it create?).
4. Decision matrix weighted by independent deployability, data consistency needs, and team ownership fit.
5. Recommendation with deciding criterion, and the seams you would cut first.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every entity in my list is owned by exactly one service per map.
- No service pair requires distributed transactions in the recommended map — or the need is explicitly called out as a cost.
- Recommendation respects the {{max_services}} cap.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Two boundary maps with ownership tables and mermaid diagrams, a per-option coupling table, pros/cons/failure modes, a weighted decision matrix, and a recommendation with first seams to cut.

prompts.title: Monolith Extraction Decision: Keep, Modularize, or Extract
prompts.description: Decide whether a monolith module should stay put, be modularized in place, or be extracted into a service — with a strangler-style extraction plan only if extraction genuinely wins.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Decide the fate of {{module_candidate}} inside {{monolith_overview}}: keep as-is, restructure as a strict module inside the monolith, or extract to an independent service.</goal>
<rationale>Extraction is expensive and mostly irreversible on a team's timeline; I need an honest comparison, not a default vote for microservices.</rationale>
<context>
- Team topology and size: {{team_topology}}
- Release cadence today: {{release_cadence}}
- Relevant incident or scaling history: {{incident_history}}
- Pain attributed to this module: {{pain_points}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- "Microservices are more modern" is not an argument; every pro must map to a stated pain or measured need.
- Do NOT assume the monolith is the problem — the null hypothesis (keep, with targeted fixes) gets a fair hearing.
- Do NOT design the target service's internal architecture; this is a boundary decision plus a migration outline.
- Quantify or flag: any claim that extraction improves deploy frequency, scaling cost, or team autonomy must cite context data or be marked as an assumption.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A decision document with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Three options (keep / modularize in place / extract), each with pros, cons, cost of change, and the failure mode.
2. Decision matrix weighted by: current pain severity, migration cost, operational burden added, reversibility.
3. Recommendation with the deciding criterion and what evidence would flip it.
4. If extraction wins: a strangler-style migration outline (seam, routing switch, data ownership transfer, rollback per step). If it loses: the top 3 in-monolith fixes instead.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- All three options seriously evaluated — no strawman "keep" option.
- Each claimed benefit traces to context data or is flagged as an assumption.
- Migration steps (if any) are each independently reversible.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A three-option decision document (keep/modularize/extract) with pros/cons/cost/failure modes, weighted decision matrix, evidence-flagged benefits, recommendation, and either a reversible strangler migration outline or top in-monolith fixes.

prompts.title: Inter-Service Communication Style Decision (REST vs gRPC vs Messaging)
prompts.description: Choose the communication mechanism for a specific service-to-service interaction by comparing synchronous REST, gRPC, and asynchronous messaging against latency, consistency, and coupling requirements.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Choose the communication mechanism for the interaction {{interaction_description}} between {{services_involved}}.</goal>
<rationale>The wrong default here either couples services into a synchronous failure chain or forces eventual-consistency complexity the business flow cannot tolerate.</rationale>
<context>
- Latency SLO for this interaction: {{latency_slo}}
- Consistency requirement: {{consistency_requirement}} (e.g. "user must see effect immediately" vs. "converges within minutes")
- Call volume / payload shape: {{volume_and_payload}}
- Team's existing tooling: {{existing_tooling}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Evaluate the mechanism for THIS interaction only; do not redesign other service communication.
- Do NOT recommend a technology because it is the org default elsewhere — restate why it fits these requirements.
- Do NOT ignore the failure path: each option must describe behavior when the callee/broker is down.
- No unquantified performance claims ("gRPC is faster") without stating the conditions under which it matters here.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A communication decision containing:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Three options — synchronous REST/HTTP, gRPC, asynchronous messaging — each with: pros, cons, failure behavior (callee down, slow consumer, poison message), and consistency semantics delivered.
2. Decision matrix weighted by: latency SLO fit, consistency fit, operational complexity, debugging/observability cost.
3. Recommendation with deciding criterion.
4. For the recommended option: the contract surface (endpoint/topic name, payload schema sketch, error or dead-letter handling) and the one fallback behavior the caller must implement.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Each option's failure behavior is described concretely, not waved away.
- The recommendation satisfies the stated latency SLO and consistency requirement, or explicitly says which requirement must relax.
- Payload schema sketch included for the recommended option.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Three communication options with pros/cons/failure behavior and consistency semantics, a weighted decision matrix, a recommendation, and a contract surface sketch with fallback behavior.

prompts.title: Write an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) from a Made Decision
prompts.description: Convert an already-made decision and its context into a clean, durable ADR that future engineers can understand without the original conversation.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Write an Architecture Decision Record for the decision "{{decision_topic}}" so that an engineer joining in a year understands what was decided, why, and what it costs us.</goal>
<rationale>The reasoning behind this decision currently lives only in chat history; when it is questioned later we will re-litigate from zero unless the context and consequences are captured now.</rationale>
<context>
- Context and forces that drove the decision: {{context_and_forces}}
- Options that were considered: {{options_considered}}
- The chosen option: {{chosen_option}}
- Known consequences so far: {{consequences_known}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- One ADR covers exactly one decision; if you detect a second hidden decision, note it as needing its own ADR — do not fold it in.
- Do NOT rewrite history: rejected options must be presented with the reasons they were plausible, not as strawmen.
- Do NOT add implementation detail (code, config); an ADR records the decision, not the build.
- Keep it in Markdown so it can live in the repo's {{adr_directory}} alongside existing records.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A single ADR file in Markdown.</deliverable>
<format>
# ADR-{{adr_number}}: {{decision_topic}}
- Status: accepted ({{date}})
- Context: forces, constraints, and the problem being solved
- Decision: the chosen option stated in one or two sentences
- Alternatives considered: each with its pros, cons, why it was plausible, and why it lost
- Recommendation rationale: a short paragraph reconstructing why the chosen option won and the criterion that decided it
- Consequences: positive, negative, and neutral — including what this decision makes harder
- Revisit triggers: conditions under which this ADR should be re-opened
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Exactly one decision recorded; hidden second decisions flagged separately.
- Every option from my context appears in "Alternatives considered" with pros and cons.
- At least one negative consequence and one concrete revisit trigger included.
- No implementation code or config snippets.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A single MADR-style Markdown ADR with status, context, decision, fairly-presented alternatives, balanced consequences, and explicit revisit triggers; hidden secondary decisions flagged.

prompts.title: Technology-Selection ADR from a Weighted Options Comparison
prompts.description: Run a disciplined technology or framework selection and produce both the comparison artifact and the ADR recording the outcome, with evidence standards that block benchmark hearsay.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Select {{thing_to_select}} for {{use_case}} and record the outcome as an ADR that survives scrutiny by engineers who were not in the room.</goal>
<rationale>This choice is costly to reverse and will be second-guessed; the record must show the comparison was evidence-based and the criteria were agreed before the winner was picked.</rationale>
<context>
- Candidate technologies: {{candidate_technologies}}
- Evaluation criteria with weights: {{evaluation_criteria_with_weights}} (e.g. operability 3x, hiring pool 2x, ecosystem maturity 2x)
- Constraints: {{constraints}} (stack, budget, compliance, team skills)
- Hard requirements (disqualifiers): {{hard_requirements}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Apply disqualifiers before scoring; a candidate failing a hard requirement is out regardless of score.
- Do NOT cite performance benchmarks, popularity stats, or "industry standard" claims you cannot ground in my context or widely documented fact — mark anything uncertain as "needs verification" with the cheapest test to verify it.
- Do NOT let the weighted total alone make the call; if the arithmetic winner feels wrong given the constraints, say so and explain.
- My stated weights are fixed; do not re-weight to favor a candidate.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>Two artifacts:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Decision table: | Candidate | Pros | Cons | Failure mode | Disqualifier check | Weighted score |, plus any "needs verification" items with a verification test each.
2. Recommendation: the winning candidate, the criterion that decided it, and the rationale in 2-3 sentences — stated BEFORE the ADR so the record leads with the conclusion.
3. An ADR (Markdown: context / decision / alternatives with pros and cons / consequences / revisit triggers) recording the winner and the strongest argument for the runner-up.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every candidate from my list appears in the table.
- Disqualifier checks applied before scoring and shown.
- Uncertain claims carry "needs verification" plus a concrete test.
- ADR names the deciding criterion and the runner-up's strongest argument.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A decision table with disqualifier checks, weighted scores, and verification-flagged claims, plus a Markdown ADR naming the deciding criterion and the runner-up's strongest argument.

prompts.title: Revisit and Supersede an Existing ADR with New Evidence
prompts.description: Evaluate whether an existing ADR still holds given changed conditions or incident evidence, and produce either a reaffirmation note or a superseding ADR with an honest postmortem of the original reasoning.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Determine whether {{existing_adr}} still stands given what has changed, and if not, produce the superseding ADR.</goal>
<rationale>Architecture decisions quietly rot as conditions change; revisiting them deliberately — with evidence — prevents both stubborn adherence and reactive flip-flopping.</rationale>
<context>
- The existing ADR: {{existing_adr}}
- What has changed since: {{what_changed}} (scale, team, requirements, ecosystem)
- Observed evidence: {{incident_or_metric_evidence}} (incidents, metrics, cost data, developer friction reports)
</context>
<boundaries>
- Treat the original decision as reasonable given its context; this is not a blame exercise — identify which assumptions stopped being true.
- Do NOT recommend change for change's sake: staying with a known-imperfect choice is a legitimate outcome if migration cost exceeds the pain.
- Every claim that conditions have changed must cite the provided evidence; do not invent trends or metrics.
- If the evidence is insufficient to decide, say so and specify exactly what measurement would settle it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A revisit assessment plus, if warranted, a new ADR.</deliverable>
<format>
1. Assessment: three options — reaffirm / amend / supersede — each with pros, cons, and cost, then a recommendation with the deciding evidence.
2. Assumption audit: | Original assumption | Still true? | Evidence |.
3. If superseding: a new ADR (Markdown: context / decision / alternatives / consequences / revisit triggers) that links the old ADR as "superseded by ADR-{{new_number}}", plus a migration-risk paragraph covering the cost of being wrong.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every original assumption appears in the audit table with an evidence verdict.
- Recommendation cites specific evidence items, not general sentiment.
- If evidence is insufficient, the response stops at the assessment and lists the measurements needed instead of forcing a verdict.
- New ADR (if any) preserves the old decision's original rationale fairly.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A reaffirm/amend/supersede assessment with an assumption-audit table tied to evidence, an honest recommendation (or an explicit insufficient-evidence stop with needed measurements), and a linked superseding ADR when warranted.

prompts.title: Event Catalog from a Business Workflow (Lightweight Event Storming)
prompts.description: Derive a clean domain-event catalog from a described business workflow, comparing fine-grained and coarse-grained event models before recommending one.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a domain-event catalog for {{workflow_description}} that engineers can implement producers and consumers against.</goal>
<rationale>We are introducing event-driven integration and need a shared, precise vocabulary of what happens in the business before choosing any broker or framework.</rationale>
<context>
- Actors involved: {{actors}}
- Systems that produce or care about these events: {{systems_involved}}
- Known downstream reactions: {{downstream_reactions}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Name events in past tense as business facts (e.g. OrderPlaced), not as commands, CRUD notifications, or technical signals.
- Do NOT select a broker, schema registry, or framework — this is the event model only.
- Do NOT invent events the workflow does not imply; if a reaction suggests a missing step, flag it as a gap question instead.
- Keep the catalog to events that cross a system or team boundary; purely internal steps belong in a separate list.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>An event catalog with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Two granularity options — fine-grained (many small events) vs. coarse-grained (fewer, richer events) — each with the full event list for that option, plus pros, cons, and the failure mode (e.g. event-churn vs. oversized payloads).
2. For the recommended option: a table | Event | Producer | Consumers | Key payload fields | Ordering sensitivity |.
3. Recommendation with the criterion that decided it.
4. Gap questions: workflow steps that are ambiguous or missing, phrased as questions to the domain owner.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- All event names are past-tense business facts.
- Every downstream reaction I listed is covered by at least one event.
- Both granularity options are complete catalogs, not sketches.
- Internal-only steps are excluded from the boundary catalog and listed separately.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Two complete granularity options with pros/cons/failure modes, a recommended event catalog table with producers/consumers/payload/ordering, a deciding criterion, and gap questions for the domain owner.

prompts.title: Event-Driven vs Request-Response Decision for a Workflow
prompts.description: Decide whether a multi-step workflow should be synchronous request-response, event-driven choreography, orchestrated, or hybrid — driven by latency, failure-tolerance, and team-experience constraints.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Choose the interaction architecture for {{workflow}}: synchronous request-response, event-driven choreography, orchestrated saga, or a justified hybrid.</goal>
<rationale>This workflow spans multiple services and the choice locks in our failure semantics, debuggability, and operational load for years; I need the tradeoffs made explicit before we build.</rationale>
<context>
- Workflow steps and services: {{workflow_steps}}
- Latency requirement: {{latency_requirements}} (does the caller block on the result?)
- Failure tolerance: {{failure_tolerance}} (what happens if a mid-workflow step fails?)
- Team experience with messaging systems: {{team_experience}}
- Existing infrastructure: {{existing_infrastructure}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT treat event-driven as the default "modern" answer; if synchronous fits the requirements, recommend it plainly.
- Do NOT hide the operational cost of messaging (broker ops, schema governance, event tracing) — price it into every async option.
- Partial failure handling must be designed, not deferred: for each option, state exactly what the user/system observes when step N fails.
- No unquantified claims like "events scale better" — tie scalability statements to the stated load or flag them as assumptions.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A decision document with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. At least three options (sync request-response, choreography, orchestration — plus hybrid if genuinely distinct), each with: pros, cons, partial-failure behavior, observability story, and failure mode.
2. Decision matrix weighted by: latency fit, failure semantics fit, operational burden, team readiness.
3. Recommendation with the deciding criterion and what requirement change would flip it.
4. For the recommended option: a mermaid sequence diagram of the happy path and the step-N-failure path.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Each option's partial-failure behavior is described concretely.
- The matrix uses my constraints, not generic best practices.
- Mermaid diagrams cover both happy and failure paths.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Three-plus interaction options with pros/cons/partial-failure behavior and observability notes, a weighted decision matrix, a recommendation with a flip condition, and mermaid happy-path and failure-path sequence diagrams.

prompts.title: Reliable Event Delivery Design: Outbox, Idempotency, Ordering, DLQ
prompts.description: Design the delivery guarantees for a critical event flow — transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, ordering strategy, retry/DLQ policy — comparing delivery-semantics options honestly.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the delivery and consumption guarantees for {{event_flow}} so that {{business_guarantee}} holds (e.g. "no payment is ever settled twice or lost").</goal>
<rationale>This event flow carries money/state we cannot afford to lose or duplicate; the design must survive broker outages, consumer crashes, and redeployments without manual cleanup.</rationale>
<context>
- Throughput and payload: {{throughput}}
- Ordering requirements: {{ordering_requirements}} (global, per-key, or none)
- Downstream consumers and their behavior today: {{downstream_consumers}}
- Broker/messaging stack in place: {{broker_stack}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT claim exactly-once delivery end-to-end; state the real guarantee each mechanism provides (at-least-once + idempotency, effectively-once within a transaction scope, etc.).
- Every guarantee must name the mechanism that enforces it and the failure window that remains.
- Do NOT redesign the whole platform; scope to this event flow, and list (without fixing) anything adjacent you notice.
- Where my inputs leave a requirement ambiguous (e.g. true ordering need), present the consequence of each interpretation rather than silently picking one.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A reliability design with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Producer side: two options for atomic state-change + event publication (e.g. transactional outbox vs. listen-to-yourself / CDC), each with pros, cons, failure window, and operational cost.
2. Consumer side: idempotency strategy (dedup keys, storage, retention) and retry policy (backoff, max attempts, DLQ contents and replay procedure).
3. Ordering: the strategy that meets {{ordering_requirements}} and its throughput cost.
4. Decision table across producer options + recommendation with deciding criterion.
5. Residual-risk list: failure scenarios this design does NOT cover, stated plainly.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Each guarantee names its enforcing mechanism and remaining failure window.
- No end-to-end exactly-once claims.
- DLQ design includes a concrete replay procedure.
- Residual risks are listed, not omitted.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Producer-side options (outbox vs CDC-style) with failure windows, consumer idempotency and retry/DLQ design with replay procedure, ordering strategy with throughput cost, a decision table with recommendation, and a residual-risk list.

prompts.title: Caching Strategy for a Hot Read Path
prompts.description: Choose a caching pattern (cache-aside, read/write-through, materialized view, or no cache) for a specific hot read path, with TTL, invalidation, and hit-rate assumptions made explicit.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the caching strategy for {{endpoint_or_query}} so that {{latency_or_load_goal}} is met without violating our staleness tolerance.</goal>
<rationale>This read path dominates database load and latency complaints; a wrong caching choice either wastes money on negligible hit rates or serves unacceptably stale data.</rationale>
<context>
- Read/write ratio: {{read_write_ratio}}
- How often the underlying data changes: {{data_change_frequency}}
- Staleness tolerance (business answer, not technical): {{staleness_tolerance}}
- Current p50/p99 latency and DB load: {{current_latency}}
- Existing infrastructure: {{existing_infrastructure}} (e.g. Redis available? CDN?)
</context>
<boundaries>
- "Add a cache" is not the default answer: if the numbers do not justify one, recommend fixing the query or adding an index and say why.
- Projected hit rates and latency improvements are estimates — flag them as assumptions and state what measurement would confirm them.
- Do NOT introduce infrastructure we do not have (per {{existing_infrastructure}}) without pricing its operational cost into the option.
- Do NOT cache data whose {{staleness_tolerance}} forbids it; call that out instead of designing around it silently.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A caching decision with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. At least three options (e.g. no cache + query optimization, cache-aside, read-through/write-through, or materialized view — as applicable), each with: pros, cons, expected hit-rate behavior, invalidation story, and failure mode (stampede, stale reads, cache-down behavior).
2. TTL and key design for the recommended option: key shape, TTL value with reasoning, invalidation triggers, and stampede protection.
3. Decision table weighted by latency gain, staleness risk, operational cost.
4. Recommendation with deciding criterion + the metrics to watch in the first week to confirm or roll back.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- No-cache option is genuinely evaluated, not a strawman.
- Hit-rate and latency projections are flagged as assumptions with a verification metric.
- Recommended option includes concrete TTL, key shape, and stampede protection.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Three-plus caching options including an honest no-cache baseline, each with pros/cons/hit-rate behavior/invalidation/failure modes, a weighted decision table, and a recommendation with TTL/key design, stampede protection, and first-week verification metrics.

prompts.title: Cache Invalidation and Consistency Design Under Real Write Paths
prompts.description: Design invalidation and consistency semantics for a cache serving multiple write paths — comparing TTL-only, event-driven invalidation, versioned keys, and write-through — with failure modes like invalidation lag and stampedes priced in.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the invalidation and consistency strategy for the cache serving {{cached_entities}} so that {{consistency_requirement}} holds across all write paths.</goal>
<rationale>Stale-data incidents erode user trust more than latency ever will; we need an invalidation design whose worst case is known and acceptable, not a hope.</rationale>
<context>
- All write paths that mutate this data: {{write_paths}} (API writes, background jobs, imports, admin tools)
- Consistency requirement per entity: {{consistency_requirement}} (e.g. "user never sees their own write stale"; "catalog can lag 5 min")
- Cache topology: {{cache_topology}} (single-region / multi-region, tiers)
- Current incident history with staleness: {{staleness_incidents}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Enumerate write paths from my list and check each against the design; a strategy that misses one write path is a failed design — say which ones are hard and why.
- Do NOT promise strong consistency from a cache architecture that cannot provide it; state the actual consistency window per option.
- Do NOT add infrastructure (streams, CDC pipelines) without pricing operational cost and listing it as a prerequisite.
- Flag any requirement in {{consistency_requirement}} that is technically inconsistent with caching, rather than designing around it silently.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>An invalidation design with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. At least three options (TTL-only, event-driven invalidation, versioned keys / write-through — as applicable), each with: pros, cons, worst-case staleness window, write-path coverage, and failure modes (invalidation lag, missed invalidations, stampedes).
2. Write-path coverage matrix: | Write path | Option A | Option B | Option C | (COVERED/GAP).
3. Decision table weighted by consistency fit, complexity, operational cost; recommendation with deciding criterion.
4. For the recommendation: concrete key/versioning scheme, invalidation message contract if event-driven, and the monitoring that detects stale-serving.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every write path from my list appears in the coverage matrix.
- Worst-case staleness is stated per option as a bound, not a vibe.
- No strong-consistency claims the mechanism cannot back.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Three-plus invalidation options with worst-case staleness bounds and failure modes, a write-path coverage matrix exposing gaps, a weighted decision table with recommendation, and a concrete key/versioning scheme plus stale-serving detection monitoring.

prompts.title: Capacity Planning and Bottleneck Analysis from Real Metrics
prompts.description: Build a quantified capacity model from current metrics and a growth projection, identify the top bottlenecks in order, and compare remediation options with costs and headroom gained.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Determine when and where {{system_description}} breaks under {{growth_projection}}, and recommend the cheapest remediation sequence that keeps us ahead of the curve.</goal>
<rationale>We need to budget next year's infrastructure and avoid both a surprise outage and panic over-provisioning; that requires arithmetic on our real metrics, not generic scaling advice.</rationale>
<context>
- Current metrics: {{current_metrics}} (traffic, latency percentiles, DB CPU/connections, queue depths, storage)
- Growth projection: {{growth_projection}} (e.g. 3x traffic in 12 months)
- Constraints: {{budget_constraints}} (budget, headcount, must-not-touch components)
</context>
<boundaries>
- Every load projection must show its arithmetic from my metrics; inputs I did not provide go into an Assumptions table with a sensitivity note.
- Do NOT recommend re-architecting before cheaper options (indexes, connection pooling, instance sizing) are evaluated and ruled out with numbers.
- Do NOT claim any component "will scale" — state its limit, the metric that reveals approaching it, and the remediation.
- Respect {{budget_constraints}} as binding; if no in-budget option meets the projection, say so explicitly instead of smuggling in an unaffordable one.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>A capacity plan with:</deliverable>
<format>
1. Capacity model: current utilization per tier, projected saturation dates (with arithmetic shown), and an assumptions table.
2. Ranked bottleneck list: | Rank | Component | Saturation point | Leading indicator metric | Time to saturate |.
3. For the top 3 bottlenecks: at least two remediation options each with pros, cons, cost, headroom gained, and implementation risk — plus a recommendation and deciding criterion.
4. Monitoring additions: the 3-5 metrics/alerts that turn this plan into an early-warning system.
</format>
<acceptance_criteria>
- All projections trace to provided metrics or flagged assumptions.
- Bottlenecks ranked by time-to-saturate, not by architectural elegance.
- Each bottleneck has >=2 remediation options with quantified headroom.
- If budget cannot meet the projection, that conclusion is stated plainly.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: A capacity model with shown arithmetic and assumptions table, a bottleneck list ranked by time-to-saturate with leading indicators, two-plus costed remediation options per top bottleneck with recommendations, and an early-warning monitoring set.

prompts.title: Failure-Mode Analysis and Graceful Degradation Design
