prompts.description: Anomaly-first isolation decision for a correctness-critical operation: concrete interleavings, engine-accurate semantics, options table, and implementation sketch with retry semantics.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Choose the correct isolation and concurrency-control strategy for {{business_operation}} on {{db_engine}} {{version}}, where correctness is money/audit-critical and throughput still matters.</goal>
<rationale>Over-serializing costs {{contention_symptom}}; under-serializing risks {{anomaly_scenario}}. The choice must be argued from the stated engine's actual anomaly semantics, not folklore.</rationale>
<context>
Operation and access pattern: {{reads_writes_and_predicates}}
Contention profile: {{concurrent_actors_and_hot_rows}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Reason from the stated engine's documented isolation semantics: which phenomena each level prevents. PostgreSQL MVCC and MySQL InnoDB differ (e.g., REPEATABLE READ phantom behavior, next-key locks) — do not conflate them.
- Do NOT assert a level prevents an anomaly without naming the mechanism (SSI/predicate locks, next-key locks, locking reads). If uncertain, mark VERIFY.
- Explicit permission: push back if my framing hides a simpler correctness mechanism (unique constraint, atomic conditional UPDATE, advisory lock).
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>
1. Anomaly analysis: which of lost update, write skew, phantom, and non-repeatable read can actually occur in this access pattern, each with the concrete two-transaction interleaving that produces it.
2. Options table: | Strategy (level + locks/constraints) | Prevents | Costs | Failure mode under contention |
3. Recommendation with the deciding criterion, an implementation sketch (SQL or ORM), and the retry semantics it requires.
</deliverable>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Each anomaly claim includes a concrete interleaving, not just a definition.
- The chosen strategy is the weakest one covering every confirmed anomaly.
- All level and lock claims are scoped to the stated engine and version.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Anomaly analysis with concrete interleavings, strategy options table with contention failure modes, weakest-safe recommendation with deciding criterion, and implementation sketch with retry semantics.

prompts.title: Model MongoDB documents: embed versus reference
prompts.description: Access-pattern-driven MongoDB document modeling with per-relationship embed/reference decisions, BSON examples, optional $jsonSchema validation, and atomicity notes.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Model the document schema for {{application_domain}} in MongoDB {{version}}, deciding per relationship whether to embed or reference.</goal>
<rationale>MongoDB schema design is driven by access patterns; defaulting to "normalize like SQL" or "embed everything" both fail at scale.</rationale>
<context>
Entities and relationships: {{entities}}
Access patterns with rough volumes: {{queries_and_cardinality}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Decide from the stated access patterns and cardinality; flag any assumed cardinality as ASSUMPTION with what evidence would change the decision.
- Respect real MongoDB constraints you can state precisely (16 MB document limit, unbounded array growth, atomicity scoped to a single document); no invented limits.
- Do NOT use $lookup joins as a default answer; justify each one from an access pattern.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>
1. Decision table: | Relationship | Embed or reference | Deciding access pattern/cardinality | Risk (growth, duplication) |
2. BSON document examples per collection (including _id strategy) showing how relationships are represented.
3. Optional $jsonSchema validation for the primary collection, valid for the stated version.
4. Update-path notes: which writes stay single-document atomic and which need multi-document handling, and how.
</deliverable>
<acceptance_criteria>
- Every relationship appears in the decision table with cardinality cited.
- No unbounded embedded array ships without a growth bound or bucketing strategy.
- Document examples are valid BSON-style JSON.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Embed/reference decision table with cardinality evidence, BSON document examples per collection, optional $jsonSchema validator, and single-document atomicity notes per update path.

prompts.title: Design a DynamoDB single-table model from access patterns
prompts.description: Access-pattern-first DynamoDB design: complete pattern-to-key matrix, PK/SK and GSI definitions with projection justification, example items, and unit-shown capacity and hot-partition analysis.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design a DynamoDB table (keys, GSIs, item layout) that serves every listed access pattern within the stated throughput.</goal>
<rationale>DynamoDB design is access-pattern-first; a missing pattern discovered after launch means a costly rebuild or table scans.</rationale>
<context>
Entities: {{entities}}
Access patterns (complete list): {{access_patterns_with_expected_rps}}
Size and throughput assumptions: {{item_sizes_and_growth}}
</context>
<boundaries>
- Every access pattern must map to a Query against the table key or a GSI; Scan is allowed only if explicitly justified as rare/admin.
- Do NOT add GSIs beyond what the patterns require; argue each GSI's projected attributes and write cost.
- Flag every capacity or partition claim derived from assumed volumes as ASSUMPTION; show RCU/WCU reasoning from stated item sizes using the real units (4 KB read, 1 KB write).
- No hot-partition hand-waving: name partition-key cardinality and per-key throughput risk explicitly.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
<deliverable>
1. Access-pattern matrix: | # | Pattern | Table/GSI | Key condition | Notes (consistency, projections) |
2. Key design: PK/SK per entity with example item collections, GSI definitions (keys, projection type), and 2-3 example items as JSON.
3. Capacity and risk section: RCU/WCU estimates from stated sizes, hot-partition analysis, and which assumptions most change the design.
</deliverable>
<acceptance_criteria>
- 100% of listed access patterns appear in the matrix; none silently dropped.
- Every GSI traces to at least one access pattern.
- Capacity math shows units and assumptions, not bare numbers.
</acceptance_criteria>
</contract>
prompts.expectedOutput: Complete access-pattern matrix with no dropped patterns, PK/SK and GSI definitions with projections, example JSON items, and unit-shown RCU/WCU plus hot-partition analysis with flagged assumptions.

prompts.title: Stack Trace Triage: Root Cause vs. Symptom
prompts.description: Diagnose a runtime exception from a verbatim stack trace, separating the root-cause frame from downstream noise before proposing a minimal fix.
prompts.prompt: Identify the single root cause of the exception below and propose the smallest fix that eliminates it. Stack traces mix the originating fault with propagation frames; fixing a symptom leaves the defect live and creates regressions elsewhere. Runtime: {{runtime_and_version}}; Framework: {{framework_and_version}}; Package manager lockfile: {{lockfile_excerpt_or_command_output}} {{full_verbatim_stack_trace}} {{implicated_files_unedited}} DO NOT propose a fix before the root cause is localized to a specific frame and line, with the quote from the trace as evidence. DO NOT paraphrase or truncate the trace in your analysis; quote frames verbatim. DO NOT suggest upgrading, reinstalling, or refactoring anything not implicated by the trace. Mention out-of-scope issues you notice in a 'Notes' section, but do not fix them. 1. Hypothesis table, ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Hypothesis | Evidence (quoted frame/code) | What would falsify this hypothesis | 2. Discriminating experiments: the cheapest checks (logs to add, inputs to try, versions to verify) that would eliminate the lower-ranked hypotheses. Order by cost. 3. Minimal fix for the surviving hypothesis, as anchored edits, plus one verification step (exact command or reproduction) that proves the fix. 4. If the provided trace/code cannot support any hypothesis, say 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' and name exactly what to collect (e.g., values at frame N, request payload, config). - Every hypothesis cites a verbatim quote from the trace or code; uncited hypotheses are invalid. - The fix targets the root-cause frame, not a catch/retry wrapper around it. - The verification step is mechanically checkable (a command plus expected output).
prompts.expectedOutput: A ranked hypothesis table with quoted evidence and falsifiers, cheapest-first discriminating experiments, one minimal anchored fix, and a runnable verification step.

prompts.title: Dependency & Version Mismatch Error Diagnosis
prompts.description: Resolve errors that smell like API/signature mismatches by verifying installed package versions first, defending against hallucinated package fixes.
prompts.prompt: Determine whether this error is caused by a version/API mismatch between my code and the installed packages, and fix it against the versions actually installed. Package APIs change across versions; guessing from training-era docs produces fixes for APIs that do not exist in the installed tree, and invented package names are a supply-chain risk. {{runtime_and_version}} {{verbatim output of npm ls / pip show }} {{full_verbatim_error_output}} {{implicated_file_and_import_block}} DO NOT recommend any package, method, or option unless it exists in the installed versions reported above. If the evidence above is missing, ask for the version command output instead of guessing. DO NOT suggest a package upgrade/downgrade unless the error proves incompatibility; if you do, name the exact target version and the evidence requiring it. DO NOT rewrite the calling code beyond the mismatch. 1. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Hypothesis (mismatch vs. logic vs. config) | Evidence quoted from error/installed versions | Falsifier | 2. Discriminating experiments: exact commands (e.g., node -e one-liners, REPL checks) that confirm which API surface is installed. 3. Minimal fix for the confirmed mismatch, with a verification step: command + expected output. 4. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch naming the exact version/log data to collect if the mismatch cannot be confirmed. - The fix references only APIs verifiable from the installed version evidence. - Any version-change recommendation names one exact version and its justification. - Verification step is a runnable command with expected output.
prompts.expectedOutput: Ranked hypothesis table distinguishing version mismatch from logic/config faults, REPL-level discriminating commands, and a fix constrained to the installed API surface.

prompts.title: Cascading Failure Localization in a Multi-Service Trace
prompts.description: Trace a cascading failure across service boundaries to find the originating fault rather than the loudest downstream symptom.
prompts.prompt: Localize the originating fault of a cascading failure that spans multiple services, distinguishing it from downstream symptoms it triggered. In distributed failures, the service that alerts loudest is usually a victim; patching victims adds defensive code while the true fault keeps recurring under load. {{services_and_versions}} {{verbatim_error_logs_from_each_affected_service_with_timestamps}} {{distributed_trace_excerpt_or_request_ids}} {{suspect_code_paths_if_known}} DO NOT conclude at the first error found; establish the temporal and causal order across services using the timestamps and request IDs provided. DO NOT propose retry logic, circuit breakers, or broader timeouts as 'the fix' — those are mitigations; place them in a separate 'Mitigations' note. DO NOT infer code paths not present in the provided logs/code; if a hop is unobservable, mark it UNOBSERVED and say what telemetry would cover it. 1. Failure timeline: ordered table | Time | Service | Event (quoted log line) | Causal link to prior event | 2. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Originating fault | Evidence (quoted) | What would falsify it | 3. Discriminating experiments: one targeted query/log/trace per hypothesis that isolates the origin. 4. Minimal fix for the originating service plus a verification step (replay the failing request; expected trace shape). 5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the missing hop/telemetry if the chain has gaps. - Every timeline row quotes a real log line from the inputs. - The root-cause hypothesis is upstream of all symptoms it explains; contradictions are flagged. - Fix is in the originating service; mitigations are labeled as such, not conflated with the fix.
prompts.expectedOutput: Timestamped cross-service failure timeline, ranked origin-fault hypotheses with falsifiers, per-hypothesis isolation experiments, and a fix in the originating service with replay verification.

prompts.title: Async Race Condition Diagnosis (Stale Response / Out-of-Order Completion)
prompts.description: Diagnose a JavaScript/TypeScript race where async completions arrive out of order (e.g., stale search results overwriting fresh ones) and design a fix.
prompts.prompt: Find the race condition causing {{symptom, e.g. 'stale search results overwriting newer ones'}} and fix it so the latest intent always wins. Out-of-order async completion bugs are intermittent in production and invisible in unit tests that await sequentially; the fix must enforce ordering, not add delays. {{framework_and_version, e.g. React 19 / Node 22}} {{implicated_component_or_handler_unedited}} {{steps_and_timing_that_trigger_the_symptom}} {{verbatim_console_or_network_logs_showing_out_of_order_completion}} DO NOT propose setTimeout, debounce tuning, or 'retry' as the fix — masking timing is not ordering. DO NOT rewrite the component/handler beyond the race; preserve the existing public props/API and behavior. If you spot other races not covered by the symptom, list them in 'Notes' without fixing them. 1. Interleaving analysis: a timeline showing the two (or more) competing execution orders and which observable state each produces. 2. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Race hypothesis | Evidence (quoted code/log) | What would falsify it | 3. Discriminating experiments: how to force each interleaving deterministically (e.g., controlled promise resolution in a test). 4. Minimal fix (e.g., request token/sequence guard, AbortController, state-transition check) as anchored edits, plus a verification test that fails before and passes after — paste both runs. 5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch naming what to instrument if ordering cannot be established from the logs. - The fix makes the correct outcome independent of completion order. - Verification test demonstrates fail-before/pass-after with verbatim output. - No timing constants or sleeps introduced.
prompts.expectedOutput: Interleaving timeline, ranked race hypotheses with falsifiers, deterministic reproduction experiments, and an ordering-enforcing fix verified by a fail-before/pass-after test.

prompts.title: Deadlock / Lock-Ordering Analysis
prompts.description: Analyze a suspected deadlock from thread dumps and lock-holding code, establish the lock-order cycle, and design an ordering-consistent fix.
prompts.prompt: Confirm or refute a deadlock from the thread dump below, map the lock-acquisition cycle, and fix the lock ordering without weakening correctness. Deadlock 'fixes' that remove locks or widen timeouts trade a hang for data corruption; the correct fix is a consistent global lock order evidenced by the dump. {{language_runtime_version, concurrency_primitives_in_use}} {{verbatim_thread_dump_or_goroutine_profile}} {{all_code_paths_that_acquire_the_implicated_locks}} {{workload_that_triggers_the_hang}} DO NOT remove a lock, shrink critical sections, or raise timeouts unless you first show which invariant each lock protects and prove the change preserves it. DO NOT conclude 'deadlock' without a quoted cycle from the dump: thread A holds X waits Y; thread B holds Y waits X. DO NOT refactor unrelated synchronization code; mention concerns in 'Notes' only. 1. Lock-wait graph: | Thread | Holds | Waits on | Evidence (quoted dump lines) |, then the cycle if one exists, or 'NO CYCLE — not a deadlock' with the alternative hypothesis. 2. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood (deadlock vs. livelock vs. slow lock-holder vs. resource starvation), each with a falsifier. 3. Discriminating experiments: instrumentation or stress config that would confirm the cycle deterministically. 4. Minimal fix establishing one global acquisition order, as anchored edits, with an invariant-preservation argument and a verification step (stress run + expected outcome). 5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the missing dumps/profiles if the cycle cannot be shown. - Every hold/wait claim cites verbatim dump lines. - The fix states the invariant each lock protects and why the new order preserves them. - Verification is a runnable stress/repro command with expected result.
prompts.expectedOutput: Lock-wait graph built from quoted dump lines, ranked deadlock-vs-alternatives hypotheses, a global lock-order fix with invariant arguments, and a stress-run verification.

prompts.title: Double-Submit / Duplicate-Action Race Triage
prompts.description: Beginner-friendly diagnosis of duplicate actions (double-click charges, duplicate records) deciding whether the fix belongs in the UI, API, or both.
prompts.prompt: Explain why {{duplicate_symptom, e.g. 'two orders are created when the Pay button is clicked fast twice'}} happens and fix it at the correct layer. Duplicates from rapid repeated actions are the most common concurrency bug users hit; fixing only the button leaves the API unsafe, and fixing only the API leaves poor UX. {{frontend_framework}} + {{backend_framework_and_datastore}} {{button_or_form_handler}} {{api_endpoint_handler}} {{verbatim_request_log_showing_the_duplicate_requests}} DO NOT propose disabling the button as the whole fix; treat UI mitigation and API idempotency as separate layers. DO NOT change any endpoint or handler other than the one implicated. Keep the fix small; note larger redesigns in 'Notes' without implementing them. 1. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Cause (UI double-fire, retry, missing idempotency, missing DB constraint) | Evidence (quoted log/code) | What would falsify it | 2. Discriminating experiments: one check per hypothesis (e.g., does the duplicate occur with the button disabled? does a replayed request create a second row?). 3. Fix, split into: (a) UI mitigation, (b) server-side guarantee (idempotency key or unique constraint). For each: anchored edit + verification step (exact request sequence + expected result). 4. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name what to capture (network log, DB rows) if the layer cannot be determined. - The server-side guarantee alone makes duplicates impossible, demonstrated by a replayed-request verification. - Every hypothesis cites quoted evidence from logs or code. - No unrelated endpoints modified.
prompts.expectedOutput: Ranked causes across UI/API/DB layers with falsifiers, one check per cause, and a two-layer fix (UI mitigation + idempotent server) with replay verification.

prompts.title: JavaScript Heap Leak Diagnosis from Snapshots
prompts.description: Interpret heap snapshots / allocation timelines to identify the retaining path of a leaking object and fix the leak at its retention source.
prompts.prompt: Identify what is retaining memory in this application and fix the retention at its source. Symptom-level fixes (restarting, raising heap limits) mask leaks until they crash under real load; the fix must break the retaining reference chain shown by the snapshot evidence. {{runtime_and_framework_versions}} {{heap_snapshot_comparison_summary_or_allocation_timeline: dominators, retained sizes, growth between snapshot A and B}} {{modules_owning_the_growing_object_types}} {{actions_performed_between_snapshots}} DO NOT recommend heap-limit increases, restarts, or manual gc() calls as the fix. DO NOT blame 'the framework'; every hypothesis must name a concrete retaining path: object type -> retainer chain -> owning code location. DO NOT add caching or WeakRef patterns beyond the leak site. 1. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Leak hypothesis (retaining path) | Evidence (quoted snapshot numbers/code) | What would falsify it | 2. Discriminating experiments: snapshot sequences or targeted instrumentation that confirm which retainer grows (e.g., repeat action N times, compare retained size of one type). 3. Minimal fix breaking the retaining chain (listener cleanup, cache bound, closure capture removal) as anchored edits, plus verification: the same snapshot protocol showing flat retained size — paste before/after numbers. 4. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the exact snapshot data to collect if retaining paths are ambiguous. - Each hypothesis names a full retaining path, not just an object type. - Verification repeats the original repro protocol and shows flat memory, with numbers pasted. - No resource-limit increases presented as fixes.
prompts.expectedOutput: Retaining-path-ranked hypotheses with snapshot evidence, confirmatory snapshot experiments, a retention-breaking fix, and before/after retained-size numbers.

prompts.title: Connection Pool / File Descriptor Exhaustion Analysis
prompts.description: Diagnose resource exhaustion (DB connections, sockets, file descriptors) from metrics and code, locating the acquisition site that never releases.
prompts.prompt: Find why {{resource, e.g. 'PostgreSQL connections'}} exhausts under load and restore release-without-leak behavior. Pool exhaustion cascades into total service failure; enlarging the pool only delays the cliff if a code path acquires without releasing, and hides the real defect. {{runtime, framework, datastore, pool_library_and_versions}} {{verbatim_metrics: pool_active/idle/waiting over time, ulimit, error spikes}} {{verbatim_exhaustion_errors}} {{all_sites_that_acquire_the_resource, plus_middleware_that_wraps_them}} DO NOT propose raising pool size / ulimits as the fix; list such changes only under 'Mitigations' with an explicit label. DO NOT assume the leak is in the obvious site; enumerate every acquisition site in the provided code and account for its release on ALL paths (success, exception, early return, cancellation). Mention unrelated resource risks in 'Notes' without fixing them. 1. Acquisition-site audit: | Site | Release on success? | Release on error? | Release on cancel/timeout? | Evidence (quoted code) | 2. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Leak hypothesis | Evidence (quoted code/metrics) | What would falsify it | 3. Discriminating experiments: load profile or fault injection (force an exception mid-request) that confirms the leaking path. 4. Minimal fix (scoped acquisition/try-finally/context manager) as anchored edits + verification: load test with pool metrics flat under the failing condition — paste metrics. 5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the metrics/tracing to add if sites cannot be ranked. - Every acquisition site in the provided code appears in the audit with a verdict. - The fix releases on all paths, verified by a load/fault test with pasted metrics. - Pool/limit increases are labeled mitigations, never the fix.
prompts.expectedOutput: Complete acquisition-site audit table, ranked leak hypotheses with fault-injection experiments, an all-paths-release fix, and flat pool metrics under load as verification.

prompts.title: Unbounded Growth Leak Triage (Caches, Listeners, Queues)
prompts.description: Beginner-level triage of steadily growing memory caused by unbounded collections, event listeners, or queues, with a bounded-structure fix.
prompts.prompt: Find which structure in this code grows without bound and make it bounded without changing observable behavior. 'Memory keeps growing until restart' is almost always an unbounded Map/array/listener registry; the fix is an eviction policy or cleanup hook, not more RAM. {{runtime_and_framework}} {{verbatim memory growth observations: numbers over time, how measured}} {{suspect_modules_unedited}} DO NOT suggest upgrading hardware, increasing heap, or scheduled restarts. DO NOT add a caching library; use structures already in the codebase. Preserve existing behavior for all currently-working cases; eviction must not drop live entries users can observe. 1. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Growing structure (file + variable) | Evidence (quoted code/symptom numbers) | What would falsify it | 2. Discriminating experiments: a simple measurement per hypothesis (e.g., log structure size on an interval, repeat the symptom action, observe which size climbs). 3. Minimal fix for the confirmed structure (size cap + eviction, listener removal on teardown, queue drain) as anchored edits, plus a verification step: repeat the original measurement and show the size plateaus — paste the numbers. 4. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: if no structure can be confirmed, state the one measurement to add and where. - The confirmed structure is named by file and variable with quoted code. - Verification shows a plateau under the original repro, with numbers pasted. - No new dependencies; no behavior change for live entries.
prompts.expectedOutput: Ranked growing-structure hypotheses with quoted code, one size-measurement experiment each, a bounded-structure fix, and plateau verification numbers.

prompts.title: Single Flaky Test Diagnosis
prompts.description: Beginner-friendly structured diagnosis of one intermittently failing test, classifying the flake source before touching test or code.
prompts.prompt: Determine why {{test_name}} fails intermittently and make it deterministic — by fixing the code if the code is at fault, or the test if the test is. Flaky tests train teams to ignore CI; 'rerun until green' hides real bugs. The cause must be classified before anything is changed. {{test_runner_and_version, CI_environment, OS}} {{verbatim failure outputs from at least two failing runs, plus one passing run if available}} {{the_flaky_test_unedited}} {{code_under_test}} DO NOT propose retries, longer timeouts, or test skipping as the fix. DO NOT modify the code under test until evidence shows the code (not the test) is at fault. If the failures provided are all identical, say so — identical failures are not a flake; ask for the passing-run output. 1. Hypothesis table of flake classes, ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Hypothesis (timing/await, ordering dependence, shared state, randomness/time, external resource, environment diff) | Evidence (quoted failure diffs) | What would falsify it | 2. Discriminating experiments: how to provoke each class deterministically (run with seed, run in isolation vs. suite, freeze clock, loop N times). 3. Minimal fix at the confirmed layer, as anchored edits, plus verification: the provoking experiment run N times green — paste the command and summary output. 4. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the runs/outputs to collect if classes cannot be ranked. - Classification cites verbatim differences between the provided failing and passing outputs. - Fix lands in the layer evidence supports; no retries or timeout bumps. - Verification is a repeated-run command with green summary pasted.
prompts.expectedOutput: Ranked flake-class table with verbatim failure diffs, deterministic provocation experiments, a layer-appropriate fix, and an N-run green verification.

prompts.title: Timing & Async Flake Hardening (Fake Timers, Polling, Awaits)
prompts.description: Fix a test suite's timing-based flakiness by replacing wall-clock waits with deterministic synchronization, without slowing the suite.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Eliminate timing-based flakiness from the tests below by replacing wall-clock dependencies with deterministic synchronization.</goal>
<rationale>sleep()/fixed-timeout waits are slow on fast machines and flaky on loaded CI runners; tests should wait on conditions, not clocks.</rationale>

<environment>{{test_framework_and_version, async_runtime}}</environment>
<tests>{{flaky_tests_unedited}}</tests>
<failures>{{verbatim CI failure outputs showing timeout/race symptoms}}</failures>
<helpers>{{existing test utilities, e.g. waitFor / fake timer setup}}</helpers>

<boundaries>
DO NOT increase timeout values as a fix; a raised timeout may remain as a backstop only, never the mechanism.
DO NOT introduce sleeps or polling intervals longer than the existing ones.
Follow the synchronization patterns already present in {{helpers}}; do not invent new test utility patterns.
Keep each change minimal; list other suspicious tests in 'Notes' without changing them.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Timing hazard (unawaited promise, wall-clock assertion, debounce/interval under test, animation frame) | Evidence (quoted test/failure) | What would falsify it |
2. Discriminating experiments: which run mode exposes each hazard (CPU-throttled run, --runInBand, repeated run).
3. Rewrites using condition-based waits or controlled clocks (fake timers) as anchored edits, one test at a time.
4. Verification: run the suite under the provoking mode N times and paste the summary; also paste total suite duration before/after to prove no slowdown.
5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the run data to collect if hazards can't be ranked.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- No fixed-duration waits added; timeouts only as backstops.
- N consecutive green runs under the provoking mode, output pasted.
- Suite duration not materially increased; both durations pasted.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Ranked timing-hazard table, provoking run modes, condition-based rewrites per test, and N green runs under throttling plus before/after suite durations.

prompts.title: Suite-Wide Flake Audit & Quarantine Strategy
prompts.description: Advanced audit of flake-rate data across a whole suite: cluster root causes, separate product bugs from test bugs, and set a quarantine/burn-down policy.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Turn raw CI flake data into a clustered root-cause audit and an explicit quarantine/burn-down plan that restores trust in the suite.</goal>
<rationale>Suite-wide flakiness is a portfolio problem: a few shared root causes (shared state, order dependence, infra) usually explain most flakes, and indiscriminate retries hide product bugs behind green dashboards.</rationale>

<environment>{{CI system, test runner, parallelism config}}</environment>
<flake_data>{{verbatim flake report: test names, failure rates, error signatures, dates}}</flake_data>
<config>{{test runner config, setup/teardown files}}</config>

<boundaries>
DO NOT propose blanket retry-on-failure for the suite; retries, if any, must be per-cluster policy with a justification.
DO NOT mark a test 'test bug' without evidence; failures that implicate product code must be escalated as product bugs with the quoted error signature.
DO NOT rewrite tests in this pass — this is analysis and policy; fixes are follow-up tasks derived from the clusters.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Cluster table: | Cluster | Signature (quoted errors) | Tests affected | Suspected shared cause | Evidence | Product bug or test bug |
2. Hypothesis ranking across clusters by flake-rate contribution, each with a falsifier and one discriminating experiment (e.g., run cluster in isolation, fixed seed, serial mode).
3. Quarantine plan: which tests quarantine now (criteria stated), which get immediate fixes, which escalate as product bugs.
4. Burn-down policy: flake-rate threshold, re-entry criteria for quarantined tests, and the dashboard metric to watch.
5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' branch: name the data to start collecting (seed, order, worker ID per failure) if clustering is impossible.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every cluster cites at least one quoted error signature from the data.
- Product-bug escalations are never labeled test bugs.
- Quarantine criteria and re-entry criteria are mechanically checkable numbers.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Clustered flake audit with quoted signatures, contribution-ranked hypotheses with isolation experiments, and a quarantine/burn-down policy with checkable thresholds.

prompts.title: Production Incident First-Response Triage
prompts.description: Structure the first 30 minutes of a production incident: blast radius, timeline, ranked causes, and a mitigate-before-fix decision.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Produce a first-response triage of this live incident: assess blast radius, rank likely causes, and recommend the fastest safe mitigation — before any root-cause fix.</goal>
<rationale>During an incident, the failure mode is premature root-causing while users bleed; triage must separate mitigation (restore service) from diagnosis (find the cause) and be honest about unknowns.</rationale>

<context>{{alert_text, start time, affected endpoints/metrics verbatim}}</context>
<recent_changes>{{deploys, config changes, flags in the lookback window}}</recent_changes>
<telemetry>{{verbatim error rates, latency percentiles, saturation metrics, sample logs}}</telemetry>

<boundaries>
DO NOT propose a code fix in this pass; output is triage and mitigation only. Root-cause work is a follow-up you will scope.
DO NOT assert a cause you cannot tie to quoted telemetry or a recent change; label it 'unverified'.
DO NOT recommend rollback of a change without checking whether the timeline actually supports it as the trigger.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Blast radius: what is broken, for whom, since when — each claim with quoted metric/log evidence.
2. Timeline: change events vs. symptom onset, flagging correlation gaps.
3. Cause hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Candidate cause | Supporting evidence (quoted) | Contradicting evidence | What would falsify it |
4. Mitigation options (rollback, flag off, scale, drain): fastest-safe recommendation with expected recovery signal and the criterion that decided it.
5. Data-to-collect-now list (dumps, traces, snapshots) before mitigation destroys evidence.
6. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' statement naming the missing telemetry if ranking is impossible.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every blast-radius and cause claim cites quoted telemetry.
- Mitigation recommendation names its recovery signal and deciding criterion.
- Evidence-preservation list precedes mitigation steps.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Evidence-cited blast radius and timeline, ranked cause table with contradicting evidence, a fastest-safe mitigation with recovery signal, and a preserve-evidence-first checklist.

prompts.title: Post-Incident Root Cause Analysis & Timeline Reconstruction
prompts.description: Blameless, evidence-anchored post-incident RCA: reconstruct the timeline, prove the root cause, and derive action items that address causes not people.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Produce a blameless post-incident analysis whose every claim is anchored to evidence, ending in action items that prevent recurrence.</goal>
<rationale>RCAs that assert causes without evidence produce action items that don't prevent recurrence; each link in the causal chain must be provable or explicitly marked unproven.</rationale>

<incident>{{summary, impact, duration, detection method}}</incident>
<timeline_raw>{{verbatim logs, alerts, deploy events, chat excerpts with timestamps}}</timeline_raw>
<mitigation>{{what was done and when service recovered}}</mitigation>

<boundaries>
DO NOT name individuals as causes; causes are conditions, changes, and missing safeguards.
DO NOT write 'human error' as a root cause; identify what made the error possible and what would have caught it.
DO NOT propose action items for causes not proven in the timeline; park speculative improvements in 'Ideas', clearly separated.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Reconstructed timeline table: | Time | Event | Source (quoted) |, with gaps marked UNKNOWN.
2. Root-cause hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Candidate cause | Evidence (quoted) | What would falsify it |.
3. Causal chain for the surviving hypothesis: trigger -> propagation -> detection -> mitigation -> recovery; each link rated PROVEN (quote) or UNPROVEN (what would prove it). Root-cause statement with the falsification test applied: 'if this cause were absent, would the incident still have happened?' answered from evidence.
4. Contributing factors ranked by how much they extended impact.
5. Action items table: | Item | Cause addressed | Owner role | Verification (how we know it's done) | — each tied to a PROVEN link.
6. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' section listing telemetry gaps to close.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every timeline row has a quoted source; gaps are marked, not filled by assumption.
- The root cause survives the falsification test using cited evidence.
- Every action item maps to a PROVEN causal link with a checkable done-criterion.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Source-quoted timeline with UNKNOWN gaps, a PROVEN/UNPROVEN causal chain with a falsification-tested root cause, and action items mapped to proven links with checkable done-criteria.

prompts.title: Error-Spike Triage from a Log Sample
prompts.description: Beginner-level triage of a sudden error-rate spike from a pasted log sample: group errors, find the dominant signature, and decide the next data to pull.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Explain this error-rate spike well enough to decide the next action: mitigate, escalate, or collect specific data.</goal>
<rationale>A wall of red logs hides the fact that most spikes are one dominant signature plus noise; grouping first prevents chasing the loudest error instead of the most impactful one.</rationale>

<context>{{service name, when the spike started, what changed recently}}</context>
<logs>{{verbatim log sample from the spike window, unedited}}</logs>

<boundaries>
DO NOT claim a root cause from this sample alone unless a quoted log line proves it; the deliverable is triage, not a fix.
DO NOT paraphrase log lines when grouping — quote them.
DO NOT ignore low-frequency errors that look severe (e.g., data corruption); flag them separately even if rare.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Grouped error table: | Group | Representative quoted log line | Approx. share of sample | First seen in sample | Severity guess + why |
2. Hypothesis table ranked by likelihood for the dominant group: | Rank | Candidate cause | Evidence (quoted) | What would falsify it |
3. Next-action recommendation: mitigate now / escalate to {{owning team}} / collect data — with the criterion that decided it.
4. Data-to-collect list: the exact queries, dashboards, or deploy diffs to pull next, each tied to a hypothesis it would confirm or kill.
5. 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' statement if no hypothesis can be supported from the sample.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every group and hypothesis cites verbatim log lines.
- The next action names its deciding criterion.
- Rare-but-severe errors are flagged even if not dominant.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Quoted-line error grouping with share estimates, ranked causes for the dominant group, a criterion-backed next action, and a hypothesis-linked data collection list.

prompts.title: Structured Logging Instrumentation for a Module
prompts.description: Add structured, level-appropriate logging to a module so future incidents are diagnosable, following existing logging conventions without log spam.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Instrument {{module_path}} so that the next failure in this module is diagnosable from logs alone: what happened, with which inputs (safely), and why it failed.</goal>
<rationale>Today this module fails silently or logs unstructured strings; incident triage requires correlation IDs and structured fields, and log spam or leaked secrets makes logs worse than absent.</rationale>

<conventions>Follow the logging patterns in {{reference_file_using_house_logger}} — same logger import, field names, and level usage. Do not introduce a new logging library or format.</conventions>
<context>{{module_path source, its callers, known past incident queries that logs couldn't answer}}</context>

<boundaries>
DO NOT log secrets, tokens, full payloads, or PII; log identifiers, counts, sizes, and hashes instead.
DO NOT add log lines inside hot loops above debug level.
DO NOT change any behavior or refactor code to make logging easier; instrumentation only.
Mention missing telemetry outside this module in 'Notes' without adding it.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Failure-mode hypothesis table ranked by likelihood for this module: | Rank | Likely failure mode | Evidence (quoted code/past incident) | What would falsify it | — instrumentation must target the top modes, not guesses.
2. Instrumentation plan table: | Location | Level | Event name | Fields (and why each is safe + useful) | — every row maps to a ranked hypothesis.
3. Anchored edits implementing the plan, matching {{reference_file_using_house_logger}} conventions.
4. Verification: a failing-path test or manual run that emits the new error log — paste the actual emitted line and show it contains the correlation ID and fields needed to answer the past incident queries.
5. Coverage check: each past unanswerable incident query mapped to the field(s) that now answer it. If the evidence cannot rank failure modes, state 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' and name the production data to collect first.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Emitted sample line pasted, structured, with correlation ID, no PII/secrets.
- Conventions match the reference file (same logger, field naming, levels).
- Every listed incident query maps to at least one emitted field.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Level/field instrumentation plan, convention-matching anchored edits, a pasted emitted log line from a failing path, and incident-query-to-field coverage mapping.

prompts.title: End-to-End Tracing Design for a Cross-Service Request Path
prompts.description: Design the minimal tracing/metrics instrumentation that makes a multi-service request path debuggable, with explicit cost/cardinality tradeoffs.
prompts.prompt:
<goal>Design the minimal instrumentation — spans, attributes, metrics, and log correlation — that makes the request path {{path_description, e.g. 'checkout: web -> api -> payments -> fulfillment'}} debuggable end to end.</goal>
<rationale>Today cross-service failures on this path require guessing which hop failed; but naive instrumentation explodes cardinality and cost, so every span/attribute must justify itself against a concrete debugging question.</rationale>

<context>{{services, languages, frameworks on the path; existing tracing/logging stack and versions; current propagation mechanism if any}}</context>
<pain>{{verbatim examples of past debugging sessions/incidents where the hop could not be identified}}</pain>

<boundaries>
DO NOT instrument code yet — deliverable is a design an engineer can implement in one pass.
DO NOT propose high-cardinality attributes (user IDs, full URLs, request bodies) as metric labels; mark any such field span-only or hashed, with the reason.
DO NOT assume a specific vendor; use OpenTelemetry-neutral naming unless the context above pins one.
Present 2-3 instrumentation depth options (e.g., entry/exit spans only vs. + critical internal spans vs. + baggage) with pros, cons, and cost/cardinality failure modes, then recommend one.
</boundaries>

<output_contract>
1. Failure-point hypothesis table ranked by likelihood: | Rank | Hop/mode most likely to fail next | Evidence (quoted pain/context) | What would falsify it | — instrumentation concentrates on top-ranked hops.
2. Question-driven plan: | Debugging question (from {{pain}}) | Signal that answers it (span/attribute/metric/log field) | Hop | Cardinality risk | — every signal maps to a ranked hypothesis.
3. Option table for instrumentation depth with a recommendation and the criterion that decided it.
4. Propagation design: how context crosses each boundary (headers/queues), with a gap list where propagation is currently impossible.
5. Verification design: the trace expected from one synthetic request — expected span tree as an outline — and how to assert it in staging. If pain data cannot rank hops, state 'EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT' and name the incident data to collect before instrumenting.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every proposed signal answers at least one question from {{pain}}; questionless signals are cut.
- Cardinality risks are called out per signal.
- Expected span tree for a synthetic request is specified and staging-verifiable.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Question-driven signal plan with per-signal cardinality risk, 2-3 depth options with a criterion-backed recommendation, propagation gap list, and an expected synthetic span tree.

prompts.title: Decision-Ready RFC Drafter
prompts.description: Drafts an RFC with goals/non-goals, an alternatives decision matrix, risks, and rollout plan — ambiguity is resolved via clarifying questions or marked OPEN, and estimates are ranges with confidence, never single-point commitments.
prompts.prompt:
Draft an RFC for {{decision_or_change}}.

GOAL: Produce a decision-ready RFC that lets {{audience}} approve, reject, or amend the proposal in one review cycle.
RATIONALE: {{why this decision is needed now / what breaks if we defer}}.

PROCESS: If constraints, success metrics, or the decision deadline are ambiguous, ask me up to {{max_questions}} clarifying questions in one batch and wait for answers. Anything still unresolved goes in Open Questions, marked OPEN — never papered over.

OUTPUT CONTRACT — an RFC with exactly these sections:
1. Summary (3–5 sentences; the decision requested stated explicitly)
2. Context & problem (cite the code, docs, or metrics each claim rests on)
3. Goals and Non-goals (bulleted; non-goals are binding)
4. Proposal (interfaces, data flow, migration path)
5. Alternatives considered:
   a. {{alternatives_count, e.g. '2-3'}} distinct options, each with pros, cons, and how it fails.
   b. A decision matrix weighted by {{criteria}}.
   c. One recommendation naming the single criterion that decided it — push back if my stated constraints point elsewhere.
6. Risks & mitigations
7. Rollout & rollback plan
8. Open questions (marked OPEN, each with an owner)

BOUNDARIES:
- No certainty theater: estimates and dates are ranges with a confidence level plus the assumptions they rest on.
- Do NOT invent requirements, benchmarks, or stakeholder positions; mark unknowns OPEN.
- No filler sections; omit nothing either.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every section present; every alternative has a failure mode; the recommendation names its deciding criterion; zero unmarked assumptions.
prompts.expectedOutput: A complete RFC with the 8 contracted sections, an options-and-tradeoffs decision matrix with weighted criteria, a single recommendation naming its deciding criterion, and an OPEN-questions list with owners.

prompts.title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Writer
prompts.description: Converts decision notes or a PR discussion into a strict-format ADR (Status/Context/Decision/Consequences/Alternatives) destined for the repo's decision log, without re-litigating or strawmanning rejected options.
prompts.prompt:
Write an Architecture Decision Record for {{decision}}, based on the context below.

GOAL: Capture why we chose {{chosen_option}} over the alternatives, so future contributors can understand — or deliberately overturn — the decision without re-litigating it.
RATIONALE: Decisions that live only in chat history get re-debated every quarter; this ADR becomes a permanent record in {{adr_location}}.

CONTEXT: {{discussion_notes_or_pr_link}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — an ADR in exactly this format:
# ADR-{{number}}: {{short_title}}
- Status: {{proposed_or_accepted}}
- Date: {{date}}
## Context — forces at play and constraints; cite code/docs for factual claims
## Decision — one unambiguous paragraph
## Consequences — positive, negative, and neutral, each with reasoning
## Alternatives considered — name plus a one-line honest rejection reason

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT add sections beyond this format.
- Do NOT strawman rejected alternatives; state their real strengths before the rejection reason.
- If the notes do not support a fact, mark it OPEN rather than inventing it.
- Do NOT reopen the decision in the text; record it.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: a reader can state what was decided, why, and what new information would justify revisiting — without reading any other document.
prompts.expectedOutput: A single ADR file in the exact contracted format, with honest alternative rejections, cited context claims, and OPEN markers for any unsupported facts.

prompts.title: Evidence-Cited Module Documentation
prompts.description: Writes technical documentation for a module where every behavioral claim carries a file:line citation, examples come from real call sites, and unverifiable claims are flagged UNVERIFIED instead of asserted.
prompts.prompt:
Write technical documentation for {{module_or_subsystem}} aimed at {{audience}}.

GOAL: A reader can use or modify {{module_or_subsystem}} correctly without reading its source first.
RATIONALE: {{why this doc is needed, e.g. 'three teams depend on this API and keep misusing the retry semantics'}}.

EVIDENCE RULE (most important): every behavioral claim must cite its source as path/to/file.ext:line or a doc URL. If you cannot verify a claim from the provided code or docs, omit it or mark it UNVERIFIED with what would confirm it. Never document aspirational or intended behavior as if it were current behavior.

CONTEXT: {{relevant_files_or_paths}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Overview — what it does and what it deliberately does NOT do
2. Concepts & data model, with citations
3. Usage: {{n_examples}} worked examples copied from real call sites in {{reference_files}}, not invented ones
4. Behavior contract: inputs, outputs, error cases, side effects — each cited
5. Known limitations & gotchas, citing issues/PRs where available
6. UNVERIFIED list

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT document anything outside {{module_or_subsystem}}; out-of-scope discoveries go in a final Notes section, mentioned but not expanded.
- Do NOT restate code line-by-line; document contracts and intent.
- If the doc would exceed {{length_budget}}, deliver an outline first, then write one section at a time; never truncate silently.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: zero uncited behavioral claims; every example traces to a real call site; UNVERIFIED items are explicitly listed.
prompts.expectedOutput: Module documentation whose every behavioral claim carries a file:line or URL citation, with real call-site examples and an explicit UNVERIFIED list.

prompts.title: Range-Based Delivery Estimation
prompts.description: Produces decomposed, range-based estimates (optimistic–likely–pessimistic with confidence) grounded in a numbered assumption log, plus a risk register — with hard rules against certainty theater and hidden padding.
prompts.prompt:
Produce a delivery estimate for {{feature_or_project}}.

GOAL: Give {{stakeholder}} an honest, decision-useful estimate: decomposed scope, ranged numbers, and the assumptions that would change them.
RATIONALE: Single-point estimates become false commitments; this team plans around ranges and explicit risk.

CONTEXT: {{spec_or_description}} | {{codebase_area}} | {{team_size_and_throughput_history}}

PROCESS: If scope is materially ambiguous, ask me up to {{max_questions}} clarifying questions in one batch BEFORE estimating; anything still unresolved becomes a stated assumption, not a silent guess.

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Scope decomposition — vertical slices, each crossing {{layers}} and independently demo-able
2. Per-slice estimate as a RANGE (optimistic / likely / pessimistic) with a confidence level (low/medium/high) and the assumptions it rests on
3. Risk register: top {{n_risks}} risks, each with trigger, impact on the range, and mitigation
4. Critical path and parallelizable work
5. Assumption log, numbered, so stakeholders can challenge specific entries

BOUNDARIES (hard rules):
- NO certainty theater: the headline is always a range plus confidence, never a single date or point estimate.
- NO hidden padding: buffer appears only as an explicit, labeled line item.
- Do NOT estimate work you have no information about — mark it UNKNOWN with what is missing.
- Do NOT compress the estimate to fit a hoped-for deadline; if {{deadline}} is infeasible, say so and show which scope cuts make it feasible.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every number traces to a numbered assumption; every slice is independently verifiable; each risk has a concrete mitigation.
prompts.expectedOutput: A slice-by-slice estimate with optimistic/likely/pessimistic ranges and confidence levels, a numbered assumption log, a risk register with mitigations, and explicit UNKNOWN markers for inestimable work.

prompts.title: Spec-to-Vertical-Slice Execution Plan
prompts.description: Converts an approved spec into a feature-list JSON plan of end-to-end vertical slices (each crossing all layers with an executable E2E test), with options-and-tradeoffs on sequencing and a cycle-free dependency graph.
prompts.prompt:
Turn the approved spec below into an execution plan of vertical slices.

GOAL: A sequenced build plan where each slice delivers end-to-end, demo-able functionality crossing {{layers}} — not horizontal phases (all-DB, then all-API, then all-UI).
RATIONALE: Horizontal phasing delays end-to-end feedback until the end; tracer-bullet slices surface integration risk in week one.

SPEC: {{spec_or_link}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — a feature-list JSON plan:
{ "features": [{ "id": "F01", "description": "...", "files": [...], "dependencies": [...], "status": "pending", "e2eTest": "exact steps proving the slice works end to end" }] }
Plus:
1. Sequencing rationale — where a genuine ordering decision exists, present {{2-3}} sequencing options with pros, cons, and how each fails; then recommend one and name the deciding criterion
2. Slice-size audit — any slice larger than {{max_slice_size}} gets split; show the split
3. Verification map — how each slice's e2eTest will actually be executed with {{verification_tooling}}

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT add scope beyond the spec; spec gaps go in an OPEN list, not into slices.
- Do NOT invent file paths that contradict the spec's Files & interfaces section.
- Do NOT produce slices a reviewer cannot independently verify.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every slice crosses all {{layers}}; every slice has an executable e2eTest; the dependency graph has no cycles; every spec item is covered by a slice or explicitly OPEN.
prompts.expectedOutput: A machine-readable feature-list JSON where each feature is a cross-layer vertical slice with files, dependencies, and an executable E2E test, plus a sequencing tradeoff analysis and a slice-size audit.

prompts.title: Interview-First Project Kickoff Plan
prompts.description: An interview-to-plan pattern: the model runs a structured batched interview (objectives, constraints, dependencies, risks, definition of done) and only then produces a milestone plan with ranged estimates and OPEN items.
prompts.prompt:
I want to plan {{project_or_milestone}}. Do NOT produce a plan yet — interview me first.

GOAL: Elicit enough ground truth to produce a realistic execution plan; in this phase the interview itself is the deliverable.
RATIONALE: Plans built on assumed constraints fail in review; I would rather answer fifteen questions now than re-plan in week two.

INTERVIEW PROTOCOL:
- Ask one batch of {{batch_size}} questions at a time; wait for my answers before the next batch.
- Cover, in order: objectives & success metrics; hard constraints (deadline, team, budget); technical landscape ({{systems_involved}}); dependencies and other teams; risks and known unknowns; what done looks like per deliverable.
- If an answer is vague, probe once more; if it is still unresolved, record it as OPEN rather than guessing.
- Challenge my premises where warranted (e.g. deadline vs. scope) — pushback is welcome.

AFTER the interview, produce:
1. Requirements summary — objectives, binding non-goals, constraints
2. Plan: milestones as vertical, independently verifiable increments, each with mechanically checkable acceptance criteria
3. Estimates as ranges with confidence levels and stated assumptions — no single dates presented as commitments
4. OPEN questions list, each with an owner
5. The first concrete next action

BOUNDARIES: Do NOT invent requirements, dates, or stakeholder commitments; mark anything unconfirmed OPEN. No plan until the interview is complete or I say 'draft with what you have'.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every milestone has checkable acceptance criteria; every number traces to a stated assumption; nothing in the plan contradicts my interview answers.
prompts.expectedOutput: First a batched clarifying interview; then a milestone plan of vertical increments with checkable acceptance criteria, range-with-confidence estimates, an OPEN-questions register, and one concrete next action.

prompts.title: Blameless Incident Postmortem
prompts.description: Writes a blameless postmortem with an evidence-quoted UTC timeline, 5-Whys terminating in system/process conditions (never people), quantified impact, and action items that each carry owner, deadline class, and verification method.
prompts.prompt:
Write a blameless postmortem for the incident described below.

GOAL: An organizational-learning document explaining what happened, why the system allowed it, and what will change — complete enough for a reader who was not there.
RATIONALE: Postmortems that assign personal blame suppress reporting and teach nothing; we optimize for system fixes.

INCIDENT MATERIALS: {{timeline_notes}} | {{logs_alerts_dashboards}} | {{chat_or_bridge_transcript}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — exactly these sections:
1. Summary — impact in user terms: who, what, how long, how many
2. Impact assessment — quantified where possible; mark estimates as estimates
3. Timeline — UTC; every entry backed by quoted evidence (log line, alert, message); gaps marked UNKNOWN, never interpolated
4. Root-cause analysis — 5 Whys applied to the SYSTEM and PROCESS, terminating in a fixable condition, never in a person
5. Contributing factors — what made it worse: missing alerts, runbook gaps, coupling
6. What went well — detection, response, rollback, with evidence
7. Action items — each with owner, deadline class ({{sla_classes}}), and a verification method proving completion; no 'be more careful' items
8. Lessons & OPEN questions

BOUNDARIES (hard rules):
- NO blame language: no names as causes, no 'failed to', 'should have known', or 'mistake by'; describe actions and conditions, not character.
- NO counterfactual shaming ('if only X had...').
- Do NOT assert causes the evidence does not support; label them HYPOTHESIS.
- Do NOT sanitize impact numbers.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every timeline entry has quoted evidence or UNKNOWN; every why-chain ends in a system/process condition; every action item has owner plus verification.
prompts.expectedOutput: A blameless postmortem with quoted-evidence UTC timeline, system-focused 5-Whys, honest quantified impact, and verifiable action items with owners and deadline classes.

prompts.title: Incident Timeline Reconstruction from Raw Evidence
prompts.description: Merges raw logs, alerts, and chat transcripts into one ordered UTC timeline where every row quotes its source verbatim, gaps stay visible as UNKNOWN, and zero causal interpretation is allowed.
prompts.prompt:
Reconstruct an incident timeline from the raw evidence below.

GOAL: A single ordered UTC timeline merging all sources, suitable as the Timeline section of a postmortem.
RATIONALE: During incidents, facts scatter across alerts, logs, and chat; a clean merged timeline is the foundation for root-cause work.

EVIDENCE: {{raw_logs}} | {{alerts}} | {{chat_transcript}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — a table:
| UTC time | Event | Source (verbatim quote) | Confidence |
Table rules:
- Every row quotes its source verbatim — a log line, alert text, or message; no paraphrased evidence.
- Convert all timestamps to UTC; note the original timezone if ambiguous.
- Inferred ordering (no timestamp): Confidence LOW, with the inference explained in one clause.
- Gaps: insert a row 'UNKNOWN — no evidence between T1 and T2'.

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT fill gaps with plausible-sounding events; absence of evidence stays visible.
- Do NOT interpret cause or assign fault — this document is sequence only.
- Do NOT drop events that seem irrelevant; tag them 'relevance: unclear' instead.
- Do NOT normalize or 'clean up' quoted source text.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every row carries a verbatim quote or an UNKNOWN marker; all times are UTC; the document contains zero causal claims.
prompts.expectedOutput: A UTC-ordered timeline table with verbatim source quotes per row, LOW-confidence flags on inferred ordering, and explicit UNKNOWN rows for evidence gaps.

prompts.title: Postmortem Action-Item Extractor & Hardener
prompts.description: Extracts action items from a postmortem, maps every root cause and contributing factor to at least one verifiable item, and rewrites 'try harder' items into mechanical fixes — without inventing items untraceable to a finding.
prompts.prompt:
Extract and harden the action items from this postmortem or incident review.

GOAL: A follow-through-ready list where each item is specific enough to verify completion and strong enough to actually reduce recurrence risk.
RATIONALE: Most incident action items die as vague tickets ('improve monitoring'); we ship only verifiable ones.

SOURCE: {{postmortem_or_meeting_notes}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — one row per action item:
| ID | Action (verb-first, concrete) | Category (detection / prevention / mitigation / process) | Owner | Deadline class | Verification (exact evidence proving completion, e.g. 'alert fires in staging drill') | Recurrence link (which failure mode it addresses) |
Then:
1. Coverage check — map every root cause and contributing factor in the source to at least one action item; anything unaddressed is listed OPEN with a proposed owner
2. Strength audit — flag items that are 'try harder' in disguise (no mechanism change) and propose the mechanical version: 'add a lint rule', not 'remember to'

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT invent action items that do not trace to a finding in the source.
- Do NOT produce person-as-fix items ('X will review more carefully').
- Do NOT accept unverifiable completion definitions — rewrite them.
- Do NOT silently drop source findings because they seem minor; route them to the OPEN list.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every finding maps to at least one item or is listed OPEN; every item has a mechanically checkable verification; zero person-as-fix items.
prompts.expectedOutput: A table of concrete, verifiable action items with owners and deadline classes, a coverage map from findings to items, and a strength audit converting vague items into mechanical fixes.

prompts.title: Verified Setup & First-Day Onboarding Guide
prompts.description: Creates a setup-to-first-PR onboarding guide in which every command is actually executed with pasted output — or explicitly marked NOT VERIFIED — including a verification gate and an annotated repo map.
prompts.prompt:
Create a verified setup-and-first-day onboarding guide for {{repo_or_project}}.

GOAL: A new engineer can go from zero to a running local environment and a first trivial merged change using only this document.
RATIONALE: Onboarding docs rot because steps are written from memory; every command here must be executed and evidenced, or marked NOT VERIFIED.

CONTEXT: {{repo_access}} | {{target_os}} | {{existing_docs}}

VERIFICATION RULE: For every command in the guide, run it in {{environment}} and paste the relevant output snippet inline. If you cannot run something, mark it 'NOT VERIFIED — confirm with {{team}}' rather than presenting it as working. Never claim a step works because it should.

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Prerequisites — exact versions and how to check each (command plus expected range)
2. Setup — numbered commands, each with what it does, expected output, and the top {{n_failure_modes}} failure modes with fixes
3. Verification gate — the exact commands proving the environment works ({{build_and_test_commands}}) with expected results
4. Your first change — a safe tiny task ({{first_task_example}}) walking through branch, change, test, PR, referencing {{conventions_doc_or_exemplar_pr}}
5. Where things live — annotated repo map with cited paths
6. Who to ask / where the docs live

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT include steps you have neither verified nor marked NOT VERIFIED.
- Do NOT document aspirational tooling; document what the repo actually uses, citing config files.
- Current state only; improvement suggestions go in a final Notes section.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every command has evidence or a NOT VERIFIED marker; a newcomer can reach the verification gate without external help.
prompts.expectedOutput: An onboarding guide where every command carries pasted evidence or a NOT VERIFIED marker, with prerequisites, failure-mode fixes, a verification gate, a first-change walkthrough, and a repo map.

prompts.title: New-Teammate Module Walkthrough
prompts.description: Writes a guided tour of one module: an ordered reading path with purposes, a cited glossary, an end-to-end flow trace with file:line hops, a safe first change, and cited gotchas.
prompts.prompt:
Write a newcomer's guided walkthrough of {{module_or_directory}}.

GOAL: After reading, a new teammate can navigate {{module_or_directory}}, know which files matter, and make a small change in the right place.
RATIONALE: {{why, e.g. 'two engineers join next sprint and this module has no map'}}.

CONTEXT: {{module_path}} | audience: {{experience_level}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. One-paragraph purpose — what this module does for the product, citing the code or docs the claim rests on
2. Reading path — the {{n_files}} files to read, in order, each with why this file, what to notice, and roughly how long to spend
3. Concepts glossary — project-specific terms, each with a one-line definition and a file citation
4. Data/control flow — one concrete request or event traced end-to-end through the files, with a file:line citation at each hop
5. Your first safe change — a suggested small edit, where to make it, and which test proves it worked
6. Traps — non-obvious gotchas, each cited to code or a past PR/issue

BOUNDARIES:
- Follow the documentation style of {{reference_doc}} if provided; do not invent a new format.
- Do NOT document files outside {{module_path}} except as entry/exit points of the traced flow.
- Mark anything you cannot verify from the code as UNVERIFIED rather than asserting it.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every reading-path file exists at its cited path; the traced flow has citations at every hop; zero uncited behavioral claims.
prompts.expectedOutput: A module walkthrough with an ordered reading path, cited glossary, an end-to-end flow trace with file:line hops, a safe first change with its proving test, and cited gotchas.

prompts.title: Senior-Level Architecture Overview from Code
prompts.description: Produces an evidence-first architecture overview of a whole system: component map and key data flows with citations, per-section confidence labels (VERIFIED/INFERRED/OPEN), and explicit reporting of doc-vs-code drift.
prompts.prompt:
Produce an architecture overview of {{system_or_repo}} for onboarding senior engineers.

GOAL: An accurate system map — components, boundaries, data flow, operational concerns — that a senior engineer trusts enough to navigate by.
RATIONALE: Senior onboarding fails when docs assert architecture that has drifted from the code; this document's value is proportional to its evidence.

CONTEXT: {{repo_paths}} | {{existing_diagrams_docs}} | {{deploy_configs}}

EVIDENCE & CONFIDENCE RULES:
- Every structural claim cites evidence: file path, config, or doc (path:line or URL).
- Label each section VERIFIED (traced in code), INFERRED (from naming/structure — state what would confirm it), or OPEN (unknown, with the question that would resolve it).
- Where docs and code disagree, the code wins — and the discrepancy is reported, not silently resolved.

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. System context — what it is, what it serves, external dependencies (cite deploy/infra configs)
2. Component map — responsibilities and ownership boundaries, one cited paragraph per component
3. Data flow — the {{n_flows}} most important flows traced end-to-end with file:line hops
4. Cross-cutting concerns — auth, errors, observability, deployment; where each lives
5. Known drift & tech debt, citing issues/TODOs where possible
6. OPEN questions for the team
7. Maintenance — append this overview to {{memory_file}} with instructions for keeping it current in future sessions

BOUNDARIES:
- Do NOT draw an idealized architecture; document the one that exists.
- Stay within {{length_budget}}; if it would run longer, outline first, then write section by section.
- Diagrams only as text or mermaid that cites the files summarized.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every component has at least one citation; confidence labels appear throughout; doc-vs-code discrepancies are listed explicitly.
prompts.expectedOutput: An architecture overview with cited component map and data flows, VERIFIED/INFERRED/OPEN confidence labels per section, an explicit drift report, and a persistable memory-file artifact.

prompts.title: Diff-Grounded Commit Message Writer
prompts.description: Generates a convention-compliant commit message strictly from the diff and supplied context — flagging mixed logical changes for splitting and asking rather than guessing when intent is not visible.
prompts.prompt:
Write a commit message for the diff below.

GOAL: A message following {{convention}} that lets a reviewer — and a future git-log archaeologist — understand WHAT changed and WHY without opening the diff.
RATIONALE: Our history is the audit trail for releases and incident forensics; vague messages ('fix stuff', 'updates') destroy it.

DIFF: {{diff}}
OPTIONAL CONTEXT: {{issue_or_ticket_link}} | {{one_line_intent_from_author}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Subject — {{type}}({{scope}}): imperative summary, under {{subject_limit}} characters; scope derived from the files touched
2. Body — only if the diff is non-trivial; explains WHY, not a restatement of the diff; references the ticket if provided
3. Footer — Refs: {{ticket}} and a breaking-change note if the diff alters public behavior

BOUNDARIES:
- Infer only from the diff and the provided context: do NOT invent motivation, tickets, or related work.
- If the diff mixes multiple logical changes (e.g. a fix plus an unrelated reformat), say so and propose a split instead of writing one message that hides the mix.
- If intent is genuinely not visible in the diff or context, ask me one question rather than guessing the WHY.
- Do NOT narrate mechanics line-by-line; the diff already says what.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: the subject parses against {{convention}}; every body claim is supported by the diff or provided context; mixed-change diffs are flagged, not papered over.
prompts.expectedOutput: A convention-compliant subject, a why-focused body when warranted, correct footer refs — plus a split proposal or one clarifying question when the diff is mixed or intent is invisible.

prompts.title: Evidence-Carrying PR Description Generator
prompts.description: Writes a PR description with a requirement-coverage table quoting satisfying code, a verification section where every claim carries command output or a NOT VERIFIED marker, and concrete risk/rollback steps.
prompts.prompt:
Write the pull request description for this change.

GOAL: A reviewer can approve with confidence using only this description plus the diff — they learn what, why, how it is verified, and what could go wrong.
RATIONALE: Review quality is bounded by description quality; unverifiable claims train reviewers to rubber-stamp.

CONTEXT: {{diff_or_commit_range}} | {{linked_issue_or_spec}} | {{ci_results}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT — exactly this structure:
## What & Why — 2–4 sentences; link {{issue}}; state the user- or system-visible outcome
## Requirement coverage — table mapping each requirement/acceptance criterion from {{spec_or_issue}} to where the diff satisfies it (quote the code), or NOT ADDRESSED
## How verified — for each claim, the exact command run and its verbatim result (test output, CI link, screenshot); anything not run says NOT VERIFIED
## Risk & rollback — blast radius, feature-flag/config gating, exact rollback steps
## Out of scope — related issues noticed but deliberately not changed (mention-only)

BOUNDARIES:
- Evidence over assertion: 'tested' means pasted output or a CI link, never the bare word.
- Do NOT claim coverage of requirements the diff does not touch.
- Do NOT pad with a file-by-file changelog; reviewers have the diff.
- If {{ci_results}} are missing, state what is needed rather than assuming green.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every requirement row quotes code or says NOT ADDRESSED; every verification claim carries evidence or NOT VERIFIED; rollback steps are executable as written.
prompts.expectedOutput: A PR description with a code-quoting requirement-coverage table, evidence-backed verification section, concrete risk/rollback steps, and an explicit out-of-scope list.

prompts.title: Tangled-Change Commit Splitting Plan
prompts.description: Designs a plan to split a tangled working state into ordered, single-idea commits — each with an independence proof, hunk-level grouping, exact git commands, and a byte-identical final-tree guarantee.
prompts.prompt:
Design a commit plan that turns this tangled change set into a clean, reviewable history.

GOAL: Split the working state below into {{target_commit_count}} logical commits where each commit is one idea, builds on its own, and tells the story of the change in review order.
RATIONALE: Reviewers approve small coherent commits; tangled histories hide bugs and make git bisect useless during incidents.

CURRENT STATE: {{diff_or_file_list}} | build/test: {{test_and_build_commands}}

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Commit plan — for each commit, in order: message (per {{convention}}) and one-line intent; files/hunks included (a file MAY be split across commits by hunk if it serves two ideas); independence proof — why this commit builds and passes {{test_command}} without the later ones
2. Ordering rationale — if more than one ordering is defensible, present the options with pros, cons, and failure modes, then recommend one and name the deciding criterion
3. Execution commands — the exact git add -p / restore / rebase sequence per commit
4. Risk notes — where a split could break bisectability, and the safeguard

BOUNDARIES (hard rules):
- Do NOT change the code's final content: the tree after the last commit must be byte-identical to the current state; state {{verification_command}} as the final check (it must show no diff).
- Do NOT rewrite already-pushed history without an explicit warning and my confirmation.
- Do NOT mix refactor and behavior change in one commit; if the tangle makes that impossible, stop and flag it instead.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: every commit is one idea with an independence proof; orderings are justified via tradeoffs; the final tree is verified identical to the starting state.
prompts.expectedOutput: An ordered commit plan with per-commit intent, hunk groupings, independence proofs, exact git commands, an ordering tradeoff analysis, and a byte-identical final-tree verification step.

prompts.title: Interview-to-SPEC.md (Signature Pattern)
prompts.description: The signature interview-to-spec workflow: a batched clarifying interview covering flows, UX states, edge cases, and non-goals — then a self-contained SPEC.md with named files/interfaces, binding out-of-scope, invariants, checkable acceptance criteria, and an end-to-end verification step.
prompts.prompt:
I want to build {{brief_description}}. Do NOT write the spec yet — interview me first, then produce SPEC.md.

GOAL: Convert my rough idea into a self-contained SPEC.md that a fresh session (human or AI) could implement without asking me anything.
RATIONALE: Implementation keyed on a written spec beats implementation keyed on a long chat: ambiguities get resolved explicitly instead of silently guessed.

INTERVIEW PROTOCOL:
- Ask one batch of {{batch_size}} questions at a time; wait for my answers before continuing.
- Cover: core flows and user roles; UI/UX states (loading, empty, error, success); data model and validation; edge cases ({{known_edge_cases}}); non-goals; integration points; performance or scale constraints; what done means.
- Probe vague answers once, then record them as OPEN.
- Challenge me when requirements conflict or scope exceeds {{budget_or_deadline}} — pushback is expected.

THEN OUTPUT — SPEC.md with exactly these sections:
# SPEC: {{feature}}
## Goal & rationale
## User flows (numbered, each covering the states above)
## Files & interfaces (named; new vs. modified)
## Data & validation rules
## Out of scope (explicit, binding)
## Invariants (existing behavior that must not change)
## Acceptance criteria (each mechanically checkable, e.g. 'POST /x with invalid email returns 422' — never 'works correctly')
## Open questions (marked OPEN, each with an owner)
## End-to-end verification step (the exact final check proving the feature works)

BOUNDARIES:
- NO invented requirements: anything I did not confirm is OPEN, not assumed.
- NO implementation until I approve the spec.
- Acceptance criteria must be testable as written.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: a fresh reader could implement without further questions; every criterion is checkable; out-of-scope and invariants are explicit.
prompts.expectedOutput: First a batched interview; then a complete SPEC.md in the contracted format with named files/interfaces, binding out-of-scope, invariants, checkable acceptance criteria, OPEN questions, and an E2E verification step.

prompts.title: Brief-to-Requirements Document with Checkable Criteria
prompts.description: Converts a feature brief into a requirements doc: prioritized user stories with mechanically checkable acceptance criteria across success/empty/error/permission states, binding non-goals, and ambiguities recorded as OPEN — never invented.
prompts.prompt:
Turn this feature brief into a requirements document.

GOAL: A requirements doc that engineering can estimate and QA can test against — user stories with checkable acceptance criteria, explicit non-goals, and zero silent assumptions.
RATIONALE: Vague briefs convert directly into scope creep and review churn; this document is the contract.

BRIEF: {{feature_brief}}
CONTEXT: {{product_area}} | {{constraints}} | {{stakeholders}}

PROCESS: If the brief leaves {{critical_aspects}} ambiguous, ask me up to {{max_questions}} questions in ONE batch before writing. Whatever remains unresolved is recorded as an OPEN question — never resolved by assumption.

OUTPUT CONTRACT:
1. Problem statement — the user pain, with the evidence we have ({{metrics_or_reports}})
2. User stories — 'As a {{role}}, I want {{capability}} so that {{outcome}}', prioritized per {{priority_scheme}}
