- Do NOT guess from the symptom alone: every hypothesis must cite a specific line from the evidence or code above. If the evidence is insufficient, name the ONE observation (log line, request, or code path) that would discriminate between your remaining hypotheses - do not pick one anyway.
- No rewrites, no library swaps, no "while we're here" improvements.
</boundaries>
</task>
Output contract:
1. Root cause: one paragraph, layer identified, evidence quoted.
2. Mechanism: why the symptoms follow from it - not a restatement of the symptom.
3. Minimal fix: a diff or a sketch of at most 15 lines.
4. Verification: the exact manual or automated check that proves the fix, including the reproduction that fails before it.
If multiple hypotheses survive the evidence, present them ranked with the discriminator needed for each.
prompts.expectedOutput: A single-layer root-cause verdict with quoted evidence, a mechanism explanation, a <=15-line minimal fix, a falsifiable verification step, and ranked hypotheses with discriminators when unresolved.

prompts.title: Establish a Performance Baseline Before Any Optimization
prompts.description: Sets up a repeatable measurement harness and captures baseline numbers for an app or endpoint before any optimization work begins, so every later claim has a before/after anchor.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a repeatable measurement setup and a recorded baseline for {{target, e.g. 'the /api/orders endpoint' or 'the product listing page'}} before any optimization happens.</goal>
<rationale>Optimization without a baseline is guesswork: we cannot tell a real win from noise, and we cannot defend the work later. Every future performance claim must trace back to this baseline.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT change any application code; measurement scaffolding (scripts, config) only.
- Do NOT propose optimizations in this response; observation only.
- Do NOT invent numbers. If a tool cannot run in my environment, say NOT MEASURED and give the exact command I should run.
- Use tools that actually exist: {{stack, e.g. 'Node 20 + Express'}} appropriate profilers, Lighthouse, autocannon, or curl timing as fits the target.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Runtime/framework: {{runtime_and_framework}}
Environment where I can run things: {{environment, e.g. 'local dev machine, prod-like staging'}}
What users complain about: {{symptom, e.g. 'page feels slow on mobile'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Measurement plan**: for each metric, the exact tool + command to capture it, and how many runs (with warmup) make it trustworthy.
2. **Baseline table**: | Metric | Value | Tool | Runs | Notes | — every cell filled from real output or marked NOT MEASURED with the command to fill it.
3. **Re-run script**: a single command or script I can re-execute after any change to regenerate the same table.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every baseline number is accompanied by the verbatim command used to produce it.
- At least one metric each for latency, resource cost (CPU/memory/bandwidth as applicable), and user-perceived time where relevant.
- The re-run script is copy-paste runnable and deterministic about run counts and warmup.
- Zero optimization recommendations appear anywhere in the response.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A measurement plan, a baseline metrics table with verbatim commands per number, and a re-runnable benchmark script — with zero optimization proposals.

prompts.title: Diagnose a CPU Hotspot from a Verbatim Profile
prompts.description: Interprets a pasted CPU profile or flame-graph summary (e.g. Chrome DevTools, --prof, py-spy, Clinic.js) to localize the real hotspot and design one confirming experiment per hypothesis.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Localize the actual CPU hotspot(s) in {{component, e.g. 'the checkout render path'}} from the profile below and design experiments that confirm or kill each hypothesis before any code changes.</goal>
<rationale>Profiles get misread constantly: people optimize the tallest-looking frame that is actually idle time, a dependency's internals, or a one-off GC pause. Acting on a misread profile wastes days.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Base every claim on the pasted profile data; quote the frames/percentages you rely on.
- Do NOT recommend micro-optimizations (caching property lookups, loop hoisting, etc.) unless the profile shows that line/frame is hot.
- Do NOT invent runtime internals (JIT behavior, GC heuristics) — if a mechanism is speculative, mark it ASSUMPTION and say how to verify it.
- If the profile is insufficient (too short, missing symbols, sampled during idle), say so and specify exactly what to re-capture.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Runtime & versions: {{runtime_versions}}
Profile (verbatim, unedited):
{{pasted_profile_output}}
</context>

<output_contract>
**Diagnosis table** — one row per hypothesis:
| # | Hypothesis | Profile evidence (quoted frames + %) | Confirming experiment | Expected delta if true |
Then: a ranked list of which hypothesis to test first and why (cost of experiment vs. expected payoff).
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every hypothesis cites at least one verbatim frame or percentage from the pasted profile.
- Each experiment is runnable as-is (exact tool/command or code probe) and has a numeric expected delta.
- Idle/GC/dependency frames are explicitly distinguished from application-code hotspots.
- No code fix is proposed without its confirming experiment listed first.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A hypothesis-to-experiment diagnosis table quoting verbatim profile frames, ranked by experiment cost vs. payoff, with insufficient-data callouts where the profile cannot support a claim.

prompts.title: Measurement-First Optimization Plan for a Latency-Critical Path
prompts.description: Produces a full optimization plan for a hot path where every candidate optimization carries a hypothesis, metric, experiment, and expected delta — ranked by impact/effort, with unmeasured items explicitly parked.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce an optimization plan for {{hot_path, e.g. 'the search API p95 latency'}} that meets {{target, e.g. 'p95 < 300ms under current load'}} without rewrites of {{off_limits_components}}.</goal>
<rationale>We have limited engineering time and a history of optimizations that shipped with no measurable effect. This plan exists to spend effort only where measurement says the time actually goes.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT propose any optimization whose cost distribution is unmeasured; unknowns become measurement tasks, not optimizations.
- Do NOT include style refactors, 'cleanliness' rewrites, or speculative caching without an eviction/consistency note.
- No unquantified scalability claims ('this will scale better') — every claimed win needs a before/after number or a concrete plan to obtain one. Mark anything else ASSUMPTION.
- Prefer reversible changes; flag any that are hard to roll back.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Architecture: {{architecture_summary}}
Current measurements (verbatim, if any): {{existing_measurements}}
Constraints: {{constraints, e.g. 'no new infrastructure this quarter'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Cost breakdown**: where time goes today (measured, or MEASUREMENT TASK with exact tool/command).
2. **Optimization plan table**: | Rank | Change | Hypothesis | Metric | Experiment | Expected delta | Effort | Risk/rollback |
3. **Sequence**: which items to land first and what re-measurement gates each step.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every optimization row has all columns filled; MEASUREMENT TASK rows are separate from optimization rows.
- Ranking is by expected-delta-per-effort and the rationale is stated.
- Each landed change has a defined re-measurement step against the baseline.
- Sum of expected deltas is checked against the target; if it cannot plausibly reach {{target}}, say so explicitly instead of padding estimates.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A measured cost breakdown, a ranked optimization table (hypothesis → metric → experiment → expected delta → effort → rollback), and a sequenced landing plan with re-measurement gates and an honest feasibility check against the target.

prompts.title: Interpret a Lighthouse Report Without Guesswork
prompts.description: Turns a pasted Lighthouse report into a faithful explanation of what each low score means, which audits are diagnostic vs. actionable, and what to re-run — without inventing browser internals.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Explain what this Lighthouse report actually says about {{page_url_or_name}}, separate the signal from the noise, and tell me which 2-3 findings are worth acting on first.</goal>
<rationale>Lighthouse reports invite two failure modes: cargo-culting every red audit, or dismissing the whole report. I need a faithful reading tied to my users' actual experience, not a generic checklist.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Interpret only what is in the pasted report; quote the audit values you rely on.
- Do NOT invent browser internals or rendering-pipeline mechanisms that the report does not evidence; mark any mechanism-level explanation ASSUMPTION and name how to verify it (e.g. a DevTools trace).
- Do NOT recommend fixes for audits that pass or that have negligible weight on the score.
- Note explicitly that lab scores differ from field data (CrUX/RUM) and what that means for my conclusions.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Device/throttling settings used: {{lighthouse_settings}}
Lighthouse output (verbatim JSON summary or audit table):
{{pasted_lighthouse_output}}
Audience context: {{audience, e.g. 'mostly mobile users on 4G'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **What the scores mean**: per-metric reading (LCP, INP/TBT, CLS, etc.) in plain terms tied to user experience.
2. **Priorities table**: | Audit | Reported value | Why it matters here | First verification step |
3. **Ignore list**: audits to not act on, with reason.
4. **Re-run guidance**: settings and run count for a trustworthy follow-up measurement.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every claim cites a verbatim value from the pasted report.
- Lab-vs-field caveat is stated with its implication for prioritization.
- Priority list is capped at 3 items, each with a verification step before any fix.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A faithful metric-by-metric reading quoting verbatim report values, a capped 3-item priority table with verification steps, an explicit ignore list, and re-run guidance — with lab-vs-field caveats.

prompts.title: Core Web Vitals Remediation Plan (LCP / INP / CLS)
prompts.description: Builds a remediation plan for a specific failing Core Web Vital using field/lab evidence, decomposing the metric into its sub-parts and ranking fixes by expected delta and effort.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Bring {{page_or_template}} into the 'good' threshold for {{vital, e.g. 'LCP ≤ 2.5s' / 'INP ≤ 200ms' / 'CLS ≤ 0.1'}} at the 75th percentile on {{device_class}}.</goal>
<rationale>This vital is failing in the field and it directly affects {{business_reason, e.g. 'search ranking and checkout conversion'}}. Random tweaking has not moved it; we need the metric decomposed and attacked at its actual bottleneck.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Decompose the metric into its documented sub-parts first (for LCP: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time, render delay; for INP: input delay, processing time, presentation delay) and identify which sub-part dominates using evidence, not intuition.
- Do NOT propose fixes for sub-parts we have not measured; unmeasured sub-parts become measurement tasks with exact tooling (WebPageTest filmstrip, DevTools Performance trace, web-vitals library attribution build, CrUX).
- Do NOT invent browser internals; if a proposed mechanism is uncertain, mark ASSUMPTION with a verification step.
- Must preserve: {{invariants, e.g. 'current SEO markup, ad slots, analytics events'}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Field data (CrUX/RUM, verbatim): {{field_data}}
Lab data (Lighthouse/WebPageTest, verbatim): {{lab_data}}
Stack: {{stack, e.g. 'Next.js 15, images via CMS, third-party tag manager'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Sub-part breakdown table**: | Sub-part | Current value (or NOT MEASURED + how) | Share of total |
2. **Remediation plan**: | Rank | Fix | Targets sub-part | Expected delta | Effort | Risk |
3. **Measurement loop**: how to attribute the vital per-session after each change (real-user attribution, not just lab re-runs).
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- The dominant sub-part is identified from evidence or explicitly flagged as the first measurement task.
- Every fix names the sub-part it attacks and a numeric expected delta with reasoning.
- Fixes touching third-party scripts include a consent/loading-strategy note.
- The plan states how field improvement will be confirmed (75th percentile, 28-day window or RUM), not just lab score.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A metric sub-part breakdown, a ranked remediation table with expected deltas per sub-part, and a field-attribution measurement loop confirming improvement at p75.

prompts.title: React Re-Render Investigation with Profiler Evidence
prompts.description: Investigates excessive React re-renders using verbatim React Profiler output, distinguishing wasted renders from cheap ones and prescribing minimal fixes (memoization, state colocation, context splitting) only where evidence justifies them.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Reduce wasted rendering in {{screen_or_flow, e.g. 'the dashboard filter interaction'}} so that {{interaction}} commits in under {{budget, e.g. '100ms'}} on {{device_class}}.</goal>
<rationale>The interaction feels janky and we suspect re-render storms, but past attempts sprinkled React.memo everywhere with no measurable gain and real maintainability cost. This time, evidence first.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT recommend memoization (memo/useMemo/useCallback) without Profiler evidence that the component's renders are both frequent AND expensive; memoizing cheap renders is a pessimization we have committed before.
- Distinguish: (a) components that render often but commit fast, (b) components with genuinely slow render phase, (c) cascade re-renders from state/context placement. Different problems, different fixes.
- Do NOT restructure state management wholesale; the smallest change that removes the measured waste wins.
- Must preserve: current component props APIs and {{invariants, e.g. 'existing test coverage, accessibility tree'}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
React version & stack: {{react_version_and_stack}}
React Profiler output (verbatim: ranked chart / commit list with actual durations):
{{profiler_output}}
Relevant component tree sketch: {{component_tree}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Render-waste table**: | Component | Renders per interaction | Self duration | Verdict: wasteful/cheap/slow/cascade | Evidence quoted |
2. **Fix list**: one row per verified problem — fix, why it removes THIS waste, expected commit-time delta, and what re-measurement proves it.
3. **Do-not-touch list**: components that look suspicious in the tree but are measurably fine.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every recommended fix cites verbatim Profiler numbers (render count, actual duration).
- At least one do-not-touch entry demonstrates restraint where data shows no problem.
- Each fix includes a before/after Profiler re-capture plan with the same interaction script.
- No context/state restructure is proposed unless cascade renders dominate the measured waste.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A render-waste verdict table quoting Profiler numbers, a minimal fix list with expected commit-time deltas and re-measurement plans, and an explicit do-not-touch list.

prompts.title: Bundle Analyzer Triage: Find the Dead Weight
prompts.description: Interprets a pasted bundle analyzer report (webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer, Rollup/Vite visualizer) to identify the heaviest and most unjustified bytes and rank safe removals.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Identify the top byte-saving opportunities in the {{bundle_name, e.g. 'main client bundle'}} from the analyzer output below, and rank them by size-saved vs. risk.</goal>
<rationale>Our initial JS is {{current_size}} and growing each release. We need to know what is actually in the bundle and which bytes are unjustified (duplicates, wrong-import-cost libs, accidental server code) before touching config.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Base every finding on the pasted analyzer output; quote sizes verbatim (parsed vs. gzip where available).
- Do NOT claim a dependency is 'unused' from size alone — flag candidates for a usage check and name the exact check (grep/import trace/depcheck).
- Do NOT recommend micro-optimizations of app code; this pass targets dependency weight, duplication, and mis-bundling only.
- Pin version assumptions: my installed versions are in the context; verify against them (npm ls) rather than assuming latest-package behavior.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Bundler & versions: {{bundler_and_versions}}
Installed deps (npm ls output for top suspects): {{npm_ls_output}}
Analyzer output (verbatim module list with sizes):
{{analyzer_output}}
</context>

<output_contract>
**Triage table**: | Rank | Module/dep | Size (quoted) | Category: duplicate / wrong-import / replaceable / legit-but-heavy / suspicious | Action | Verification step | Est. saving |
Then: a 'not a problem' note for heavy modules that are justified.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every row quotes a verbatim size from the analyzer output.
- 'Replaceable' suggestions name a concrete alternative and its approximate size delta, or mark the delta UNKNOWN with how to measure it.
- No action lacks a verification step (usage check or build-size re-run).
- Estimated savings are summed and stated against the current total.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A ranked triage table quoting verbatim module sizes with category, action, verification step, and estimated saving per row — plus a justified-heavy note and a total savings estimate.

prompts.title: Code-Splitting Strategy with Options and Tradeoffs
prompts.description: Designs a code-splitting / lazy-loading strategy by enumerating viable split-point options (route, interaction, vendor) with pros, cons, failure modes, and a decision matrix weighted by the project's criteria.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Decide a code-splitting strategy for {{app_description}} that gets the initial-load JS under {{budget, e.g. '200KB gzip'}} while keeping {{critical_interaction, e.g. 'first search keystroke'}} feeling instant.</goal>
<rationale>The current single-bundle approach blows the budget, but naive splitting trades load time for interaction latency waterfalls and cache churn. This is an architecture decision with real failure modes, so enumerate options before recommending.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT propose splitting everything by default; every split point costs a network round trip and cache fragmentation — justify each one.
- Do NOT claim bundle-size outcomes without measuring; size claims must come from the analyzer data provided or be marked ASSUMPTION with a verification command.
- Respect the stack: {{stack, e.g. 'React Router + Vite'}} — propose only mechanisms that stack actually supports (dynamic import, route-level lazy, manualChunks as applicable).
- Must preserve: {{invariants, e.g. 'SSR for the landing page, existing prefetch behavior on nav hover'}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Current bundle breakdown (verbatim analyzer summary): {{bundle_breakdown}}
User flows by frequency: {{flow_frequency, e.g. '90% land on home, 30% open settings'}}
Decision criteria & weights: {{criteria, e.g. 'initial load 50%, interaction latency 30%, cache hit rate 20%'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Options**: 2-3 viable splitting strategies; each with pros, cons, and how it fails.
2. **Decision matrix**: options x weighted criteria, scored.
3. **Recommendation** with the deciding criterion named, plus the concrete split-point list (what loads eagerly, lazily, and on which trigger, including prefetch hints).
4. **Verification plan**: build-size and interaction-timing measurements to confirm the budget after implementation.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Each option has an explicit failure mode (e.g. waterfall on slow networks, cache invalidation churn).
- The recommendation names the single criterion that decided it and pushes back if my weights point elsewhere.
- Every lazy boundary lists its loading UX (skeleton/spinner/none) and prefetch trigger.
- Verification plan includes both a bundle-size check and a real interaction-latency measurement.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: 2-3 splitting strategies with pros/cons/failure modes, a weighted decision matrix, one recommendation with concrete split points + prefetch triggers, and a two-pronged verification plan.

prompts.title: Image and Static Asset Optimization Pass
prompts.description: Audits image/font/media delivery for a page or app — formats, sizing, lazy-loading, font loading — producing a fix list where each item cites measured transfer sizes and targets a specific metric.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Cut image and static-asset transfer weight on {{page_or_template}} from {{current_weight}} toward {{target_weight}} without visible quality regression or layout shift.</goal>
<rationale>Assets are {{asset_share, e.g. '70% of page weight'}} and dominate LCP and data costs for mobile users. But blind 'compress everything' passes have caused quality complaints and CLS regressions before.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Every finding must cite a measured transfer size from the provided evidence (network waterfall, coverage report, or asset inventory); no assumed sizes.
- Do NOT recommend format transcodes (AVIF/WebP) without noting browser-support fallback behavior and the actual byte delta per asset.
- Do NOT change hero/LCP images to lazy loading — explicitly check for and flag that anti-pattern if present.
- Must preserve: visual quality bar defined by {{quality_bar, e.g. 'no visible artifacting at 2x DPR'}} and zero new CLS.
- If a fix requires build tooling we don't have ({{build_stack}}), name the tool and config delta, don't hand-wave it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Asset inventory / waterfall (verbatim): {{asset_evidence}}
Build stack: {{build_stack}}
Device/DPR mix from analytics: {{device_mix}}
</context>

<output_contract>
**Fix table**: | Rank | Asset/class | Current size (quoted) | Fix (format/resize/srcset/font-display/etc.) | Est. saving | Metric affected (LCP/CLS/bandwidth) | Quality risk |
Plus: a font-loading plan (subsetting, font-display, preload) as its own section, and a per-page re-measurement checklist.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every row quotes a measured current size.
- The LCP image is explicitly identified and its loading strategy stated (eager + fetchpriority, never lazy).
- Font plan prevents both invisible-text flash and layout shift, or explains the accepted tradeoff.
- Savings are summed vs. the target; shortfalls are stated honestly with what else would be needed.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A ranked asset fix table with quoted sizes and estimated savings, a dedicated font-loading plan, explicit LCP-image handling, and an honest savings sum against the target.

prompts.title: HTTP Caching Headers Audit and Design
prompts.description: Audits current Cache-Control/ETag behavior from verbatim response headers and designs a correct header policy per asset class, including invalidation mechanics and verification curl commands.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design a correct HTTP caching policy for {{origin_or_app}} covering {{asset_classes, e.g. 'static assets, HTML pages, API GET responses'}} and fix the misconfigurations found in the audit.</goal>
<rationale>We currently either under-cache (repeat visitors re-download everything, origin load spikes) or over-cache (users see stale deploys). Both are production incidents we've had. The fix must be per-asset-class and verifiable with curl.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Base the audit on the verbatim response headers provided; do not assume CDN/framework defaults — mark any default-behavior claim ASSUMPTION with a curl command to verify.
- Never recommend caching personalized or auth-dependent responses without an explicit Vary/private strategy; if any endpoint's personalization is unclear, flag it as MUST VERIFY, don't guess.
- Every cached class needs an invalidation story (fingerprinted URLs, short TTL + revalidation, or explicit purge) — no unbounded TTLs on mutable content.
- Do NOT invent CDN-specific header behavior; stick to standard semantics unless I confirm the CDN ({{cdn}}).
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Current response headers per asset class (verbatim curl -i output): {{response_headers}}
Deploy/fingerprinting setup: {{deploy_setup}}
CDN: {{cdn}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Audit table**: | Asset class | Current headers (quoted) | Verdict: under-cached / over-cached / broken-revalidation / OK | Risk |
2. **Target policy table**: | Asset class | Cache-Control + validators | Invalidation mechanism | Verification curl + expected response |
3. **Rollout order**: safest-first sequence with what to watch (hit-ratio, staleness reports) after each step.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every verdict quotes the current header values verbatim.
- Every target policy includes a copy-paste curl verification command with the expected headers/status (200 vs 304).
- Auth-dependent or personalized responses are either excluded with reason or given an explicit private/Vary design.
- No policy lacks an invalidation mechanism.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: An audit table with verbatim headers and verdicts, a per-class target policy with invalidation mechanisms and curl verification commands, and a safest-first rollout order.

prompts.title: Multi-Layer Caching Architecture Decision
prompts.description: Chooses where caching belongs across browser/CDN/app/datastore layers by enumerating options with consistency failure modes, a weighted decision matrix, and explicit staleness budgets per data type.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design the caching architecture for {{system_description}} so that {{performance_goal, e.g. 'p95 read latency < 80ms and origin QPS drops 10x'}} while never violating {{consistency_requirement, e.g. 'a user always sees their own writes within 1s'}}.</goal>
<rationale>We have ad-hoc caching at some layers and none at others, causing both stale-data bugs and avoidable origin load. Caching is a consistency-vs-speed tradeoff, so the layers and TTLs must be chosen deliberately, not accreted.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT add a cache layer without naming its invalidation mechanism and its worst-case staleness; 'cache it in Redis' without an eviction story is a rejected answer.
- No unquantified claims ('this will scale'); every layer's benefit needs an expected hit-rate/latency/QPS figure marked MEASURED (from provided data) or ASSUMPTION with a plan to measure it.
- Enumerate 2-3 coherent architecture options before recommending; include the failure mode of each (stampede, stale reads after write, dual-write inconsistency, cache-penetration).
- Must preserve: {{invariants, e.g. 'no PII in shared caches, session correctness'}}
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Data types and access patterns: {{data_access_patterns}}
Current measurements (verbatim): {{current_measurements}}
Decision criteria & weights: {{criteria, e.g. 'consistency 40%, latency 30%, ops complexity 30%'}}
Existing infra: {{infra}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Options**: 2-3 layer combinations; pros, cons, failure modes each.
2. **Decision matrix** weighted by my criteria; recommendation + deciding criterion; push back if my weights point elsewhere.
3. **Per-data-type policy table**: | Data type | Layer(s) | TTL/strategy | Invalidation trigger | Worst-case staleness | Consistency guarantee met? |
4. **Measurement plan**: hit-rate, latency, and staleness metrics to instrument before and after.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every cache layer in the recommendation has an invalidation mechanism and a stated worst-case staleness.
- The consistency requirement is explicitly proven or flagged as at-risk per data type.
- Benefits are quantified and labeled MEASURED or ASSUMPTION-with-plan.
- Failure modes (stampede/stale-read/penetration) are addressed for the recommended option specifically, not generically.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: 2-3 caching architecture options with failure modes, a weighted decision matrix with pushback, a per-data-type policy table (TTL, invalidation, worst-case staleness), and an instrumentation plan.

prompts.title: Diagnose a Stale-Content or Cache-Miss Bug
prompts.description: Debugs a concrete caching bug (users see stale content, or cache never hits) from verbatim headers, requests, and versions — localizing the layer at fault before proposing the minimal fix.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Find which cache layer is causing {{bug_symptom, e.g. 'users see yesterday's prices after deploy' / 'every request misses the CDN cache'}} and identify the minimal fix.</goal>
<rationale>Caching bugs get 'fixed' by adding more caches or flushing everything, which hides the fault and creates the next incident. Localize the misbehaving layer first, then fix only it.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Distinguish the layers explicitly: browser cache, service worker, CDN edge, application cache, database query cache. The evidence must identify ONE faulty layer before any fix is proposed.
- Do NOT paraphrase or reinterpret the headers/responses I pasted; quote them verbatim in your reasoning.
- Do NOT propose 'clear all caches' or 'disable caching' as the fix — at most as a temporary mitigation clearly labeled MITIGATION, not FIX.
- Do NOT invent CDN/framework caching defaults; mark ASSUMPTION and give the exact command or config lookup to verify.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Symptom & when it started: {{symptom_and_timeline}}
Verbatim request/response pairs (curl -i or HAR excerpts, including re-requests): {{request_response_evidence}}
Relevant config (service worker / CDN rules / app cache code, unedited): {{config_excerpts}}
Versions: {{versions}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Layer elimination table**: | Layer | Evidence for | Evidence against | Verdict: ruled out / suspect / faulty |
2. **Root cause**: the specific header/config/logic at fault, quoted.
3. **Minimal fix**: the smallest config/code change, with the curl or browser steps that prove it (expected headers/status on first vs. second request).
4. **Regression check**: how to detect this class of bug in CI or monitoring going forward.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Exactly one layer is named faulty, with quoted evidence; other layers explicitly ruled out.
- The fix is provable via a described request sequence with expected response codes/headers.
- No 'flush everything' appears except as a labeled temporary MITIGATION.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A layer-elimination table, one quoted root cause, a minimal fix with a request-sequence proof, and a regression detection check.

prompts.title: Slow Query Diagnosis from EXPLAIN Output
prompts.description: Reads verbatim EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE output for a slow query, identifies the true bottleneck (scan type, row misestimates, join order), and proposes the smallest index or query change with a before/after plan.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Make {{query_description, e.g. 'the order-history query'}} meet {{latency_target, e.g. 'p95 < 50ms'}} by fixing what the query plan proves is wrong — nothing more.</goal>
<rationale>This query is our top database time consumer. Past attempts added indexes speculatively, bloating write amplification without helping. The plan output below is the ground truth; the fix must follow from it.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Base the diagnosis on the pasted EXPLAIN output; quote the specific nodes, costs, row estimates vs. actuals you rely on.
- Do NOT recommend an index without stating its write cost and which existing indexes become redundant.
- Do NOT rewrite the query's semantics; result shape and filtering behavior must be identical. Must preserve: {{invariants, e.g. 'ORM-generated SQL shape where possible'}}.
- Do NOT invent database internals (planner heuristics, storage layout); mark uncertain mechanisms ASSUMPTION with a test to verify (e.g. ANALYZE, extended statistics).
- If the plan provided lacks ANALYZE/actual rows, say what to re-run ({{db_engine}}-appropriate: EXPLAIN ANALYZE / EXPLAIN PLAN + tkprof / etc.) before prescribing.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
DB engine & version: {{db_engine_version}}
Table sizes & cardinalities: {{table_stats}}
The query (unedited): {{query_sql}}
EXPLAIN output (verbatim): {{explain_output}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Plan reading**: what the plan actually does, node by node for the expensive nodes only, with quoted numbers.
2. **Bottleneck verdict**: the single dominant cost driver and its evidence; row-estimate vs. actual mismatches called out.
3. **Fix options** (smallest first): index-only / query-shape / statistics — each with expected plan change, write-amplification cost, and rollback note.
4. **Before/after protocol**: exact commands to re-measure (same parameters, warm vs. cold cache stated).
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- The bottleneck verdict cites verbatim plan nodes and numbers.
- Each fix states its cost (write amplification, index size, migration risk).
- The before/after protocol controls for cache warmth and parameter selectivity.
- If evidence is insufficient, the response leads with the re-measurement command, not a guess.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A focused plan reading with quoted nodes, one evidence-backed bottleneck verdict, smallest-first fix options with write costs, and a cache-controlled before/after measurement protocol.

prompts.title: N+1 Detection and Elimination with Query-Count Evidence
prompts.description: Finds and fixes N+1 query patterns using query-log or APM evidence, choosing per-case between eager loading, batching, and caching, with query-count before/after as the acceptance metric.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Reduce the query count per request on {{endpoint_or_job, e.g. 'GET /api/feed'}} from {{current_query_count}} toward {{target_query_count, e.g. '<= 5'}} by eliminating N+1 patterns proven in the evidence below.</goal>
<rationale>Latency and DB load scale with row count on this path, and it degrades as data grows. But blanket eager loading has previously made things worse (giant joins, over-fetching), so each fix must match its access pattern.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Every N+1 claim must cite the verbatim query log/APM trace showing the repeated statement and its count per request.
- Do NOT eager-load everything: for each case choose deliberately among eager loading, dataloaders/batching, a projection/join, or a small cache — and state why that choice fits the access pattern and cardinality.
- Do NOT change response shape or pagination semantics. Must preserve: {{invariants, e.g. 'API contract, authorization filters per record'}}.
- Watch for the opposite failure: fixes that replace N small queries with one query fetching unused columns/rows must be flagged with the over-fetch cost.
- No unquantified claims: each fix lists expected query-count delta; total expected count must be stated after all fixes.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
ORM/framework & versions: {{orm_and_versions}}
Query log / APM trace for one request (verbatim): {{query_log}}
Relevant models/associations: {{model_excerpt}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **N+1 inventory**: | # | Repeated statement (quoted) | Count/request | Source (code location) | Access pattern |
2. **Fix table**: | # | Chosen strategy | Why it fits | Query-count delta | Over-fetch/perf risk | Code sketch |
3. **Verification**: exact way to count queries per request before/after (test or log assertion), with the expected after-count per fix.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Each inventory row quotes the repeated SQL and its observed count.
- Each fix names its strategy and justifies it against cardinality; authorization-per-record filters are preserved or explicitly addressed.
- The after-state query count is computed and compared to the target; shortfalls are stated, not hidden.
- A query-count regression test or assertion is part of the deliverable.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: An N+1 inventory quoting repeated statements, a per-case strategy-justified fix table with query-count deltas and over-fetch risk flags, and a query-count regression check.

prompts.title: Endpoint Latency Budget Breakdown
prompts.description: Allocates an end-to-end latency budget across an endpoint's stages (auth, DB, external calls, serialization) from tracing evidence and identifies which stage overruns, with per-stage fixes ranked by delta/effort.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Get {{endpoint, e.g. 'POST /api/checkout'}} p95 from {{current_p95}} to {{target_p95}} by finding which stage(s) blow the budget and fixing only those.</goal>
<rationale>Total latency is known but stage-level attribution is not; teams keep optimizing the stage they own rather than the stage that matters. A budget forces honest attribution.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Attribute time across stages from the provided trace/telemetry evidence; stages without data are MEASUREMENT TASKS with the exact instrumentation to add (span names, timers), not guesses.
- Do NOT propose optimizing any stage whose measured share is under {{noise_floor, e.g. '5%'}} of p95.
- Do NOT blame external services without their measured latency distribution; if downstream latency is unmeasured, the first action is measuring it (and noting timeout/retry behavior).
- Serialization, middleware, and framework overhead get the same scrutiny as DB time — no favorites.
- Every fix needs an expected p95 delta and a before/after re-measurement against the same percentile and load conditions.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Trace/telemetry evidence (verbatim spans, timings, logs): {{trace_evidence}}
Stage map (what happens in this endpoint): {{stage_map}}
Percentiles available: {{percentiles, e.g. 'p50/p95/p99 from APM'}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Budget table**: | Stage | Measured p95 contribution (or NOT MEASURED + instrumentation) | Share % | Budget | Overrun? |
2. **Fix list** for overrunning stages only: | Fix | Expected p95 delta | Effort | Risk |
3. **Instrumentation gaps**: exact spans/timers to add where attribution is missing.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Contributions sum to the observed p95 within a stated tolerance; unexplained residue is called out, not silently dropped.
- No fix targets a stage below the noise floor.
- p95 (not averages) is used throughout; averages-only evidence is flagged as misleading and re-queried.
- Each fix has a same-conditions re-measurement plan.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A stage-level budget table summing to observed p95 with residue called out, fixes only for overrunning stages with expected deltas, and a concrete instrumentation gap list.

prompts.title: Load Test Design with k6/Artillery (Realistic Traffic Model)
prompts.description: Designs a load test scenario that models realistic traffic (arrival rates, think time, auth, data variance) with thresholds as pass/fail gates — explicitly rejecting 'hammer one endpoint with max VUs' anti-patterns.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a runnable {{tool, e.g. 'k6'}} load test for {{system_under_test}} that answers: {{question, e.g. 'does checkout stay under p95 800ms at 3x Black-Friday average traffic?'}}.</goal>
<rationale>Past load tests were max-VU hammers on one endpoint: they produced impressive-looking failure numbers that predicted nothing about production. A test that doesn't model real traffic shape answers a question nobody asked.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Model realistic traffic: arrival-rate-based (not just closed-model VUs where the tool supports it), per-endpoint weights from {{traffic_distribution}}, think time, session/auth flows, and variance in payload/data (no single cached-hot user).
- Do NOT test against production without explicit written approval gates; default target is {{environment, e.g. 'staging with prod-scale data'}} and say what differences vs. prod bias the results.
- Do NOT report averages as the result; thresholds are p95/p99 latency + error rate. Define thresholds BEFORE running, as pass/fail gates in the script.
- Include warmup and a ramp that distinguishes 'breaks at X RPS' from 'never warmed up'.
- If a realism factor can't be modeled (e.g. real third-party payment latency), mark it ASSUMPTION and state its directional bias on results.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Stack & endpoints: {{stack_and_endpoints}}
Traffic shape (analytics-derived): {{traffic_distribution}}
Auth mechanism: {{auth_mechanism}}
Environment: {{environment}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Scenario design**: stages, arrival rates, endpoint weights, data variance strategy — each justified against the stated question.
2. **Runnable script** ({{tool}}) with thresholds as codified pass/fail gates.
3. **Result interpretation guide**: which metrics answer the question, what distributions to plot, and the known biases (environment deltas, ASSUMPTION list).
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- The script runs as-is with {{tool}} and encodes p95/p99 + error-rate thresholds.
- Traffic weights trace back to the provided distribution; deviations are justified.
- Warmup and ramp stages are present and explained.
- The interpretation guide lists every known bias between this test and production reality.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A justified scenario design, a runnable k6/artillery script with codified p95/p99 and error-rate thresholds, and a result-interpretation guide listing production-vs-test biases.

prompts.title: Capacity Plan from Load Test Evidence
prompts.description: Turns load test results into a capacity plan: knee-point identification, headroom math, bottleneck resource attribution, and scaling options with honest extrapolation limits.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a capacity plan for {{system}} answering: what load can we serve within {{slo, e.g. 'p95 < 500ms, <0.1% errors'}}, what breaks first, and what {{growth_event, e.g. 'launch, 5x traffic'}} requires.</goal>
<rationale>Capacity decisions are currently made on vibes and one hero load test. Scaling the wrong resource wastes money; scaling late causes the outage. The plan must follow from measured behavior, including where the measurements stop being trustworthy.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Ground every capacity claim in the provided load test data (verbatim numbers); extrapolation beyond measured load is allowed only as labeled EXTRAPOLATION with its error bounds and assumptions stated — never presented as fact.
- Identify the knee: the load at which latency/errors depart from linear, from the data — not a round-number guess.
- Attribute the bottleneck resource (CPU, DB connections, memory, I/O, downstream) from resource metrics correlated with the knee; if resource telemetry is missing, the first action is instrumenting it, marked MEASUREMENT TASK.
- No unquantified scalability claims ('adding replicas fixes it') — each scaling option states which resource it relieves and what new bottleneck appears next.
- Costs: include rough cost implications per option where determinable, marked ASSUMPTION otherwise.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>
Load test results (verbatim: RPS/latency/error series, resource metrics): {{load_test_data}}
Current topology & instance specs: {{topology}}
Cost constraints: {{cost_constraints}}
</context>

<output_contract>
1. **Behavior summary**: latency/error vs. load, with the knee identified and quoted.
2. **Bottleneck verdict**: resource + evidence; next-in-line bottleneck stated.
3. **Capacity table**: | Load level | Measured/EXTRAPOLATION | SLO met? | Limiting resource |
4. **Scaling options**: 2-3, each with resource relieved, next bottleneck, cost implication, and a decision recommendation with deciding criterion.
5. **Re-test plan**: what to re-measure after each scaling change.
</output_contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- The knee and all capacity numbers are quoted from the data or labeled EXTRAPOLATION with assumptions.
- The bottleneck is tied to resource metrics, not inference from latency alone.
- Each scaling option names the bottleneck it creates next.
- The plan states what load level we can confidently serve today, in one unambiguous sentence.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A knee-point analysis with quoted data, a resource-evidenced bottleneck verdict, a measured-vs-extrapolated capacity table, scaling options with next-bottleneck and cost, and a re-test plan.

prompts.title: Modernize One Legacy Function with Proven Behavior Parity
prompts.description: Safely modernize a single legacy function (e.g., callbacks to async/await) with a smallest-possible diff and a before/after behavior-parity proof.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Modernize {{legacy_function}} in {{file_path}} to {{modern_idiom, e.g. 'async/await with typed errors'}} while producing the smallest reviewable diff.</goal>
<rationale>This module is {{why_it_matters, e.g. 'on the checkout hot path'}}; modernization reduces defect rate, but any behavior drift ships straight to production.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT modify any file other than {{file_path}}.
- Do NOT change the function's name, signature, return shape, thrown error types, or observable side effects (logging, network calls, event emission).
- Do NOT reformat, rename, or reorganize any code outside {{legacy_function}}.
- Do NOT add dependencies, helpers, comments, or docstrings.
- If you spot unrelated issues, list them under 'Notes' but do NOT fix them.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Quote the current implementation of {{legacy_function}} verbatim.
2. The refactored implementation as an anchored edit:
FILE: {{file_path}}
<<<< ANCHOR (verbatim existing lines) / ==== (replacement) / >>>> END
3. A before/after comparison table mapping every observable behavior (inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, ordering) to prove parity.
4. Notes section: out-of-scope findings only.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- {{test_command}} passes; paste the verbatim output.
- {{typecheck_or_lint_command}} passes.
- Diff touches only {{legacy_function}} inside {{file_path}}.
- Every row in the comparison table marked IDENTICAL, or explicitly flagged as an intended behavior change that requires my approval before you apply it.
</acceptance_criteria>

Behavior preservation is the entire job. If you cannot prove a behavior is unchanged, mark that row 'UNVERIFIED — needs test' instead of claiming parity.
prompts.expectedOutput: Verbatim quote of the original function, one anchored edit, a before/after behavior-parity table with IDENTICAL/UNVERIFIED rows, pasted test/lint output, and a Notes section for out-of-scope findings.

prompts.title: Characterization Tests Before Touching a Legacy Module
prompts.description: Build a characterization-test safety net that pins current behavior (including bugs) of an under-tested legacy module before any modernization begins.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Create a characterization-test safety net for {{legacy_module}} that pins its CURRENT behavior — including suspected bugs — so later refactors can be proven behavior-preserving.</goal>
<rationale>{{legacy_module}} has {{coverage_situation}}; without pinned behavior, any 'refactor' here is an unverifiable rewrite.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT modify {{legacy_module}} or any production code. Test files only.
- Do NOT fix, document, or 'improve' surprising behavior you discover — characterize it as-is and flag it.
- Do NOT refactor the module to make it testable; use only seams that exist today (current constructor args, existing dependency injection points, module-level mocks in {{existing_test_stack}}).
- Do NOT add test-framework dependencies beyond {{existing_test_stack}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
Phase 1 (this response): inventory the public surface of {{legacy_module}} — quote each exported signature verbatim — and propose the behavior list to pin: happy paths, edge cases ({{known_edge_cases}}), error paths, and observable side effects. Do NOT write test code yet; wait for my approval of the list.
Phase 2 (after I approve): write the tests in {{test_file_path}}, run them, and paste the verbatim output. Any test failing against current code is a discovered behavior: mark it `@characterization: surprising` and stop for my decision.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every public export has at least one pinned-behavior test, or an explicit reason it is untestable without source changes.
- Full suite green with verbatim output pasted; surprising behaviors flagged, never fixed.
- Coverage report for {{legacy_module}} attached as evidence.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A quoted public-surface inventory, an approved behavior-pinning list, then a characterization test file with verbatim run output; surprising behaviors marked and reported, not fixed.

prompts.title: Staged Legacy Modernization Campaign Plan (No Big-Bang)
prompts.description: Plan a multi-file modernization (e.g., class components to hooks, callbacks to async/await) as independently shippable, reversible slices with a decision table for strategy.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce a staged modernization plan for migrating {{subsystem}} from {{legacy_pattern, e.g. 'callback-style async with event emitters'}} to {{target_idiom, e.g. 'async/await with structured errors'}} across ~{{file_count}} files — without a big-bang rewrite.</goal>
<rationale>{{business_reason}}; previous attempts failed because the change was attempted in one PR. Every step must be independently shippable and reversible.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Plan only: do NOT write production code in this phase.
- Do NOT bundle framework/language upgrades into this program; one axis of change at a time.
- No step may touch more than {{max_files_per_step}} files or break the build if merged alone.
- If a file cannot be modernized without behavior risk, mark it DEFER with the blocking reason instead of forcing it in.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
Deliverable: MODERNIZATION.md containing:
1. Inventory table: file | pattern instance count | one quoted representative snippet | test coverage | risk (H/M/L).
2. Strategy decision table: 2–3 approaches (codemod + manual cleanup / file-by-file manual / adapter-first) with pros, cons, and failure modes, weighted by {{criteria: team size, release cadence, rollback needs}}; one recommendation and the criterion that decided it.
3. Slice plan: ordered steps, each = change → verification gate ({{test_command}} + {{typecheck_command}} green) → rollback procedure (exact revert scope). Lowest-risk, highest-coverage files first.
4. Interop rules: how old-style and new-style code coexist mid-migration, and the invariant that keeps the mixed state safe.
5. Done definition: mechanically checkable completion criteria.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every step passes its gate independently; no step changes observable behavior without an explicit, separately approved flag.
- Whole plan reviewable within {{review_budget}}; every inventory row backed by a quoted snippet.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A MODERNIZATION.md with an evidence-backed inventory, weighted strategy decision table with one recommendation, an ordered slice plan (change → gate → rollback per step), interop invariants, and checkable done criteria.

prompts.title: Introduce a Design Pattern into Conditional Dispatch
prompts.description: Replace a sprawling switch/if-else dispatch with a named pattern (e.g., Strategy) as one bounded diff with a dispatch-parity table.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Replace the {{conditional_sprawl, e.g. 'switch statement dispatching on payment type'}} in {{file_path}} with the {{pattern_name, e.g. 'Strategy'}} pattern, as one small reviewable diff.</goal>
<rationale>Every new {{case_type}} currently edits this function, causing merge conflicts and regressions; the pattern isolates each variant.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT change which branch executes for any input — dispatch behavior must be identical, including default/fallback handling and error cases.
- Do NOT apply the pattern anywhere else in the codebase, even where it would also fit.
- Do NOT add interfaces or abstractions beyond what {{pattern_name}} minimally requires; no 'for future flexibility' hooks.
- Follow the conventions in {{reference_file}} for naming, file layout, and typing; introduce no pattern absent from it.
- Mention unrelated code smells under Notes; do NOT fix them.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Quote the code being replaced, verbatim.
2. Anchored edit(s): FILE / <<<< ANCHOR / ==== / >>>> END blocks.
3. Before/after dispatch table: for each input case, old branch → new handler, marked IDENTICAL or FLAGGED (FLAGGED requires my approval before applying).
4. Notes.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- {{test_command}} passes — paste verbatim output. If test coverage of the dispatch is thin, say so explicitly and list the untested cases instead of claiming safety.
- {{typecheck_or_lint_command}} passes.
- Existing callers keep working unchanged; no caller-side edits in this diff.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Verbatim quote of the replaced dispatch, anchored edits following the reference file's conventions, an IDENTICAL/FLAGGED dispatch-parity table, and pasted test/lint output including honest coverage gaps.

prompts.title: Pattern-or-Not Decision with Options and Tradeoffs
prompts.description: Decide whether a problem area needs a design pattern at all — comparing 2–3 options including a no-pattern minimal refactor via an evidence-based decision matrix.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Decide whether and how to restructure {{problem_area}} — which currently suffers {{symptom, e.g. 'a 400-line method with five responsibilities'}} — as an evidence-based design decision, not a default pattern application.</goal>
<rationale>{{why_now}}; the wrong abstraction here adds indirection that outlives its usefulness, so the decision must be grounded in this code, not in fashion.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT write implementation code; this is a decision phase.
- 'Do not apply a pattern — minimal refactor only' MUST be one of the options; patterns are not the goal.
- Do NOT recommend anything requiring new dependencies or framework adoption.
- Base every claim on the quoted code, never on generic best practice.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Quote the key sections of the code under discussion, verbatim.
2. Enumerate {{2-3}} viable options (the no-pattern option included). For each: pros, cons, how it fails in {{codebase_context}}, and which evidence in the quoted code supports or undermines it.
3. Decision matrix weighted by {{criteria: team familiarity, expected change frequency, test coverage}}.
4. One recommendation, the criterion that decided it, and the smallest first step to validate it: a reversible single-file change with its verification gate ({{test_command}}).
5. If my constraints point away from my stated preference, say so explicitly and show why.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every option traced to quoted code; 'industry standard' alone is never accepted as justification.
- The recommended first step is independently revertible and verifiable.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Quoted code, a 2–3 option comparison with pros/cons/failure modes (including a no-pattern option), a weighted decision matrix, one recommendation with deciding criterion, and a reversible validation step.

prompts.title: Remove a Misapplied Pattern (De-Abstraction)
prompts.description: Collapse an unjustified abstraction layer (e.g., a factory with one implementation) into concrete code, with usage evidence first and fresh-context verification after.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Remove the misapplied {{pattern_name, e.g. 'abstract factory'}} layer in {{module_paths}} and inline it to the {{simpler_form, e.g. 'two concrete constructor calls'}} actually used — collapsing indirection without changing behavior.</goal>
<rationale>The abstraction wraps {{actual_variant_count}} real variant(s) and has seen no new implementations in {{years}} years; it costs every reader a detour and every change a multi-file edit.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Sequence as independently mergeable steps; never one big-bang deletion.
- Do NOT change any behavior: wiring order, lazy vs eager instantiation, error propagation, and lifecycle are preserved exactly.
- Do NOT delete public types while any consumer outside {{module_paths}} imports them — deprecate in place instead.
- No speculative re-abstraction ('a simpler base class for later'); collapse to concrete code.
- Out-of-scope discoveries go to Notes only.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Usage evidence FIRST: quote every implementation and every call site (verbatim grep results) proving the variant-count premise. If the evidence contradicts the premise, stop and report — do not refactor.
2. Slice plan: step → change → verification gate ({{test_command}} + {{typecheck_command}} green, verbatim output) → rollback (revert scope).
3. Execute ONLY step 1 this session, as anchored edits.
4. Then review the step-1 diff with a fresh-eyes stance: assume behavior changed; for each call site prove UNCHANGED by quoting the before/after code path, or flag SUSPECT.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Step 1 green with pasted outputs; review table all-UNCHANGED or explicitly flagged.
- Zero imports of removed symbols remain (paste grep evidence).
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Grep-verified usage evidence, a slice plan with gates and rollbacks, step-1 anchored edits only, a UNCHANGED/SUSPECT per-call-site verification table, and zero-remaining-imports evidence.

prompts.title: Evidence-Backed Tech-Debt Inventory
prompts.description: Produce a debt inventory where every item carries quoted code evidence and a concrete cost mechanism — no fixes, no style opinions, no unverifiable claims.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Produce an evidence-based tech-debt inventory for {{target_area}} that separates verified debt from style preference.</goal>
<rationale>The team currently debates debt from memory; a list where every item is backed by quoted code or measurable cost is the only kind that survives prioritization review.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT fix anything — inventory only.
- Do NOT list style disagreements (naming, formatting) as debt unless they violate {{lint_config}}.
- Do NOT recommend rewrites; each item gets a remediation class, not a project.
- If evidence for a suspected item cannot be produced from the code, mark it UNVERIFIED instead of asserting it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
Deliverable: a debt table, one row per finding:
| ID | Location (file:line) | Debt (quoted code evidence) | Concrete cost (defect history, change friction, performance, security) | Severity (H/M/L) | Effort (S/M/L) | Remediation class (refactor / test-gap / upgrade / delete) |
Filling rules:
- Quote the actual code in every row — no row without evidence.
- Severity must cite a mechanism (e.g., 'this null path caused INC-{{ticket}}'), never an adjective.
- Cap at the top {{max_items}} items, ranked by severity × change frequency.
Close with a 'Suspected but unverified' list; for each entry name the exact command or file that would verify it.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every H-severity row has quoted evidence; the diff contains zero fixes; a reviewer can spot-check every row by file:line.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A spot-checkable debt table (every row with quoted code and a cost mechanism), capped and ranked, plus a 'Suspected but unverified' list with the verification path per item.

prompts.title: Tech-Debt Paydown Plan with Cost-of-Delay Sequencing
prompts.description: Turn a debt inventory into a sequenced, independently mergeable paydown plan scored by cost of delay, with risky items gated on characterization tests.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Turn the debt inventory in {{debt_inventory_artifact}} into a sequenced paydown plan where every work item is independently mergeable and behavior-preserving by construction.</goal>
<rationale>{{planning_context}}; debt work competes with features, so items must be small enough to ship between feature work and justified by cost of delay, not taste.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Planning only: do NOT implement any item.
- Do NOT bundle unrelated debts into one 'cleanup' item — each item gets its own verification gate and rollback.
- Any item whose fix could change observable behavior is flagged RISKY and gated on characterization tests first.
- Respect the freeze list: {{do_not_touch_areas}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Scoring: rank each inventory item by cost of delay (change frequency × blast radius × risk), reusing the quoted evidence from the inventory; show the score computation, not just the result.
2. Sequenced plan: per item — step → exact change scope → verification gate ({{test_command}} green, verbatim output at execution time) → rollback procedure. Order: high severity, low effort, high coverage first.
3. Explicit 'not now' list with the criterion that excluded each item.
4. Session-0 shortlist: the {{n}} items to execute first, each sized under {{max_pr_size}}.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every planned item traces to an inventory row ID; every gate is mechanically checkable; dependencies between items are stated, never implicit.
- If my preferred ranking contradicts the cost-of-delay evidence, push back explicitly and show the numbers.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A scored ranking with visible computation, a sequenced plan (step → scope → gate → rollback per item), an argued 'not now' list, and a session-0 shortlist of PR-sized items.

prompts.title: Hotspot Analysis: Churn × Complexity Targeting
prompts.description: Find refactoring targets that actually hurt by combining git churn, complexity, and coverage evidence — targets vs monitor vs ignore, with data-quality caveats.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Identify the refactoring targets in {{repo_or_directory}} where debt actually hurts, using change-frequency and complexity evidence instead of intuition.</goal>
<rationale>Refactoring effort is finite; ugly code nobody touches is cheap, while hot files compound debt cost every sprint.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Analysis only — do NOT modify code.
- Use only evidence you produce with commands; paste the exact commands and outputs (e.g. `git log --name-only --since='{{window}}'`, {{complexity_tool}} output). No remembered or assumed hotspots.
- Do NOT equate complexity with debt: a complex file with near-zero churn is a MONITOR, not a target.
- Do NOT produce full fix plans; per target, a remediation class and first slice only.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Churn data: top {{n}} files by change frequency over {{window}}, with the verbatim command and output.
2. Complexity/size data for the same set via {{complexity_tool}} (or LOC proxy), verbatim output.
3. Hotspot table: file | churn | complexity | test coverage | verdict (TARGET / MONITOR / IGNORE) | one-line mechanism for the verdict.
4. Per TARGET: remediation class and the smallest first slice with its verification gate ({{test_command}}) and rollback.
5. Data-quality caveats: what the evidence cannot show (squashed history, generated files, recent renames).
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every TARGET verdict is backed by BOTH churn and complexity numbers from pasted outputs; any file recommended without both is flagged INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Verbatim churn and complexity command outputs, a TARGET/MONITOR/IGNORE verdict table with mechanisms, first slices for targets, and explicit data-quality caveats.

prompts.title: Strangler-Fig Migration Plan (Seam Map to Decommission)
prompts.description: Design a route-by-route strangler-fig migration: seam map, reversible slices behind facades/flags, parity-evidence plan, interop invariants, and decommission criteria.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Design a strangler-fig plan to migrate {{capability, e.g. 'the reporting module'}} from {{legacy_system}} to {{target_system}} incrementally, seam by seam, with the old system decommissionable at the end and reversible at every stage.</goal>
<rationale>{{why, e.g. 'legacy framework is end-of-life'}}; a cutover rewrite has failed here before ({{failure_history}}), so the migration must deliver value per slice and never leave both systems in a broken mixed state.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Plan only; no implementation code this phase.
- No big-bang cutover step anywhere: every slice shifts one narrow seam (one route, endpoint, or job) and is independently reversible.
- Do NOT redesign the domain model or rename concepts mid-migration; migration fidelity first. List redesign temptations under 'Deferred'.
- Data-consistency rules during dual operation must be explicit; no silent dual-writes without a reconciliation story.
</boundaries>
</task>

<context>Paste the current wiring and relevant code excerpts (route registrations, queue consumers, cron jobs, config) here: {{current_wiring_or_code_context}}</context>

<contract>
Deliverable: MIGRATION.md with:
1. Seam map: interception points ({{seam_types, e.g. 'router, queue consumers, cron jobs'}}) with current wiring quoted verbatim from {{current_wiring_or_code_context}}; if a seam's wiring is missing from the context, mark it OPEN instead of inventing it.
2. Slice plan: ordered slices, each = scope → facade/flag mechanism → verification gate ({{test_command}} + {{smoke_check}} green) → rollback (flag off / exact revert scope).
3. Interop invariants: what must hold while both systems serve traffic (data ownership per entity, idempotency, ordering).
4. Equivalence-evidence plan: how each slice proves parity before its flag flips (shadow traffic, response diffing, fixture replay).
5. Decommission criteria: mechanically checkable conditions for deleting legacy code.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Each slice is shippable alone; rollback never requires deploying to {{legacy_system}}; every parity claim names a concrete evidence mechanism.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A MIGRATION.md with a quoted seam map, ordered reversible slices with gates and flag-based rollbacks, interop invariants, a per-slice parity-evidence mechanism, and checkable decommission criteria.

prompts.title: Execute One Strangler-Fig Slice with Parity Proof
prompts.description: Implement a single approved migration slice behind a flag/facade, with fixture-replay parity evidence before cutover and a rehearsed rollback.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Execute slice {{slice_id}} of the strangler-fig migration in {{migration_doc}}: move {{seam, e.g. 'GET /reports/:id'}} to {{target_system}} behind the {{facade_or_flag}} mechanism, with parity proven before any cutover.</goal>
<rationale>This slice is next in the approved plan; executing it as one bounded, reversible step is what keeps the migration from becoming a big-bang.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Execute ONLY slice {{slice_id}}; later slices, other routes, and any redesign are out of scope (Notes only).
- Flag default = legacy path. The new path stays dark until I flip it.
- Do NOT change the response contract: status codes, headers, payload shape, and error bodies must be byte-comparable unless an approved exception exists in {{migration_doc}}.
- No changes to {{legacy_system}} beyond the minimal interception hook; legacy must keep working if the new path is deleted.
- If parity evidence contradicts the plan's assumptions, stop and report — do not improvise around it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Quote the current legacy handling of the seam, verbatim.
2. Anchored edits for the interception hook and the new-path implementation, following patterns in {{reference_file_target}}.
3. Parity evidence: run {{parity_check, e.g. 'fixture replay diffing legacy vs new responses'}} over {{fixture_set}} and paste the verbatim diff result. Zero unexplained diffs = proceed; otherwise stop.
4. Completion report table: build / tests / flag-defaults-off / scope — each PASS/FAIL with verbatim evidence.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- {{test_command}} and {{typecheck_command}} green with verbatim output pasted; flag defaults to legacy; rollback (delete new files + flag off) demonstrated.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Quoted legacy seam handling, anchored edits, verbatim fixture-replay parity output, and a checklist completion report; flag defaults to legacy with rollback demonstrated.

prompts.title: Verify-and-Decommission Legacy Code After Migration
prompts.description: Prove a migrated legacy component is truly dead (traffic, imports, registrations, config) and remove it in reversible slices — evidence before deletion.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Verify that {{legacy_component}} is truly dead and decommission it safely — removal as a sequence of reversible steps, not a celebratory bulk delete.</goal>
<rationale>Premature deletion of 'unused' legacy code is a top cause of migration rollbacks; removal must be proven by evidence, not assumed from the migration plan.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Do NOT delete anything until the liveness evidence in step 1 is produced and reviewed.
- Do NOT remove shared utilities still referenced elsewhere — prove per-symbol with grep.
- Removal proceeds in slices, each with its own gate; no single 'delete legacy/' commit.
- Keep {{monitoring_or_kill_switch}} in place for {{grace_period}}; removing the kill-switch is the LAST slice.
- On any discovery of live usage: stop, quote the call path, report — do NOT patch around it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Liveness evidence (verbatim commands + outputs): zero traffic in {{telemetry_source}} over {{window}}; zero imports (grep); zero queue/cron registrations; zero references in config/infra ({{iac_paths}}). Any nonzero result = STOP and report.
2. Removal slice plan ordered by blast radius (registrations/config → entry points → internals → shared leftovers); each = change → gate ({{test_command}} + {{build_command}} + {{deploy_smoke_check}} green, verbatim) → rollback (revert scope; restore from VCS).
3. Execute slice 1 only; paste gate outputs.
4. Post-slice fresh-eyes check: assume something still references the deleted code; prove the negative with quoted search evidence.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Every liveness check shows zero with pasted evidence; slice 1 fully green; rollback rehearsed (revert + smoke check) before I approve slice 2.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Zero-result liveness evidence across traffic/imports/registrations/config, a blast-radius-ordered removal plan, slice-1 execution with pasted gates, and a prove-the-negative reference check.

prompts.title: Convert One JavaScript File to TypeScript, Zero Runtime Change
prompts.description: Single-file JS→TS conversion with strict-compatible types, caller-compatibility proof, baseline-vs-after typecheck evidence, and no runtime edits.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Convert {{js_file}} to TypeScript with strict-compatible types and zero runtime behavior change, as one reviewable diff.</goal>
<rationale>This file is on the {{migration_initiative}} critical path; the conversion must be safe to merge without a feature freeze.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Rename to .ts/.tsx and add types; do NOT restructure logic, reorder statements, rename identifiers, or 'fix' bugs you notice (Notes only).
- No `any` unless the JS is genuinely untypeable without a refactor — then use `unknown` plus a TODO stating the blocker, capped at {{max_unknown}} occurrences.
- Do NOT change runtime constructs: no enum-for-object swaps, no class conversions, no optional-chaining 'cleanups'. Types are erased; runtime is not.
- Do NOT add type packages or edit tsconfig; use {{existing_types_setup}}.
- Public export signatures must stay call-compatible with all current JS callers — verify with grep.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Capture the baseline FIRST: run {{typecheck_command}} before changing anything and paste the error count.
2. Quote the original file's exports verbatim.
3. The converted file (anchored edits, or the full file if anchors are impractical — state which and why).
4. Caller-compatibility table: each export × each call site (grep evidence) → UNAFFECTED / NEEDS-CAST (flagged for my approval).
5. Notes.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- {{typecheck_command}} after conversion shows zero NEW errors versus the pasted baseline.
- {{test_command}} green, verbatim output.
- Emitted-JS check via {{build_and_diff_method}} confirms runtime semantics unchanged apart from type erasure.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: Baseline typecheck output, verbatim export quotes, the converted file, an UNAFFECTED/NEEDS-CAST caller table with grep evidence, and after-vs-baseline typecheck plus test output.

prompts.title: Eliminate `any` Incrementally with Evidence-Traced Types
prompts.description: Replace listed `any`/loose-type sites with precise types in green-at-every-slice batches; every new type justified by quoted data-shape evidence.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Reduce unsafe typing in {{ts_area}} by replacing the `any`/loose-type sites listed below with precise types, in slices that each keep the build green.</goal>
<rationale>`any` here defeats the type system exactly at the {{risk_area}} boundary; tightening must be incremental because one strict change cascades through callers.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Work ONLY on the listed sites: {{any_site_list_or_grep_output}}. Newly discovered `any`s elsewhere: Notes, do NOT touch.
- Type-level changes only; runtime behavior identical. If a site cannot be typed without a runtime change, mark it BLOCKED with the quoted reason and move on.
- No tsconfig changes, no new type dependencies, and no `as any` / `@ts-ignore` / `@ts-expect-error` as a 'fix' — that relocates the problem instead of remediating it.
- Follow the type conventions in {{reference_types_file}} (generics style, narrowing approach); introduce no pattern absent from it.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
Slice plan first: group the sites so each slice compiles alone. Per slice: sites → exact type replacements → verification gate ({{typecheck_command}} zero-new-errors vs the baseline you capture first; {{test_command}} green) → rollback (revert the slice).
Then execute slice 1 only. For each site: quote the current code, show the replacement type, and cite the evidence justifying that shape ({{evidence_source, e.g. 'API schema / sample payload / generated db types'}}) — no invented shapes.
Close with the remaining-`any` count delta, backed by grep output.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- Baseline-vs-after typecheck counts pasted; slice 1 fully green; every introduced type traced to quoted evidence; BLOCKED sites listed with reasons.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A compile-safe slice plan, slice-1 execution with per-site quoted evidence for each new type, baseline-vs-after typecheck counts, and a grep-backed remaining-any delta.

prompts.title: Strict-Mode Enablement Campaign with Per-Package Ratchet
prompts.description: Plan and pilot a path to strict TypeScript across a repo: baseline error census, strategy decision table, one pilot package taken green, and a reusable ratchet template.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Plan and pilot a path to `strict: true` ({{strict_flags}}) for {{repo_scope}}, which currently compiles with {{current_config}} — as a per-package campaign with a ratchet, not a flag flip.</goal>
<rationale>Flipping strict globally produces {{estimated_error_count}} errors and stalls; a package-by-package ratchet lands progress permanently while main stays green.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Phase 1 (this response): plan plus a pilot on ONE package, {{pilot_package}}. Do NOT touch other packages or the root tsconfig beyond what per-package overrides require.
- No mass suppression: `@ts-expect-error` is allowed only as a tracked, counted ratchet with an owner and issue link per batch — never as the primary strategy.
- No runtime changes to satisfy the compiler without a flagged, separately approved exception. Strict errors that reveal real bugs go to a follow-up list with quoted evidence.
- No new dependencies or tsconfig bases beyond {{existing_setup}}.
</boundaries>
</task>

<contract>
1. Baseline: enable the strict flags for {{pilot_package}} only; paste the verbatim error count and a categorized sample (quote one error per category).
2. Strategy decision table: fix-all-now vs suppression-ratchet vs boundary-typing-first — pros, cons, failure modes, weighted by {{criteria}}; one recommendation and the deciding criterion.
3. Pilot execution: apply the chosen strategy in error-category slices; per slice: change → gate ({{typecheck_command}} + {{test_command}} green, verbatim) → rollback.
4. Campaign template: the repeatable per-package checklist plus a PROGRESS.md format so later sessions can continue the ratchet without this conversation.
</contract>

<acceptance_criteria>
- {{pilot_package}} strict-green with pasted evidence; suppression count reported with issue links; root build green throughout.
</acceptance_criteria>
prompts.expectedOutput: A verbatim baseline error census with categories, a weighted strategy decision table, a strict-green pilot package with per-slice gates, and a PROGRESS.md ratchet template for future sessions.

prompts.title: Single Dependency Major-Version Upgrade, Changelog-Verified
prompts.description: Upgrade one package across a major version: usage inventory, pre-upgrade adaptations, the bump, residual fixes — every code change traced to a quoted changelog entry.
prompts.prompt:
<task>
<goal>Upgrade {{package_name}} from {{current_version}} to {{target_version}} in {{project_path}}, adapting our code to breaking changes with small, verifiable steps.</goal>
<rationale>{{driver, e.g. 'CVE fix / end-of-life / required feature'}}; major upgrades fail when the version bump and code adaptations land as one unreviewable diff.</rationale>
<boundaries>
- Verify against ground truth before changing code: paste `npm ls {{package_name}}` output, quote the breaking-change entries from the official {{target_version}} changelog/migration guide, and grep our usage sites. Do NOT migrate APIs from memory — if a change is not in the official notes, it does not happen.
- Sequence: (1) usage inventory, (2) adaptations that work on BOTH versions where possible, (3) the version bump, (4) residual fixes. Each step has its own gate.
- Do NOT upgrade other packages 'while here'; lockfile churn beyond {{package_name}} and its required peers is out of scope.
- No behavior changes beyond what the migration guide mandates; behavioral deltas introduced by the new version must be flagged for my explicit approval.
</boundaries>
</task>
